content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

BalletX brought its unique brand of contemporary ballet to The Joyce Theater last week.  In a program of three ballets – Beautiful Once, Macaroni and Heroes – these excellent dancers moved effortlessly among diverse dance and theatrical styles with impressive technique and exquisite grace.

Beautiful Once celebrates the grandeur and simplicity of connection in sweeping gestures and clean lines, making a dance of even a simple embrace.  Rooted in classical vocabulary, the dance is nevertheless contemporary in shape and feel.  Jodie Gates’ choreography and Ryan Lott’s music echo each other in pleasing legato and bright staccato.  The piece opens with a pas de deux, which turns into two and then three, as couples enter the stage and slowly fill it with movement, building a pastiche of memory.  Each phase of a friendship, or love – each effortless lift, each floating leap — evolves organically.  It creates a harmony of continuous movement that is so satisfying.  Subsequent pas de deux and pas de trois elaborate on the theme, in a variety of emotional colors.  In their simple costumes of fawn brown or gray chiffon, the dancers are by turns fleet and winsome, soulful and dramatic.

The second piece Macaroni, offers a complete, and delightful, contrast.  A seditious ‘amuse bouche’ that puts the ‘dandy’ in Yankee Doodle, Macaroni celebrates 18th century European queer culture and the flamboyant men who comprised it.  Mocked as overdressed, tea-drinking arrivistes with their racquetball and foppish affectations, these men were referred to derogatorily as “macaronis.”  The song Yankee Doodle Dandy threads its way throughout the piece in a perfect reference point, as what I assume most of us wouldn’t know (I certainly did not), its lyrics are actually an insult to ignorant Americans who would think sticking a feather in one’s hat would make one fashionable, like a Macaroni.  (Yup, too dumb even to be successfully bourgeois.)  These proto-drag queens, as it were, were derided because they were – let’s face it – fabulous.  Costumer Emma Kingsbury leans in to the fabulous with bright color and ornate plumage, both figurative and literal.  The dancers appear in neon chartreuse unitards, each with a silkscreened image of an 18th century portrait, short waistcoats and sporting matching chartreuse wigs.  This camp aesthetic perfectly translates Loughlan Prior’s inventive, quirky choreography, creating a layered, free-spirited Yankee Doodle of the absurd.

The final piece of the evening was Heroes, in which Choreographer Takehiro Ueyama honors the Japanese men and women who picked up the pieces of their shattered, post World War II country and transformed it into a thriving economy with re-invigorated culture.  Deeply emotional and abstract, Heroes looks inward as it builds outward.

The dancers dance barefoot, in simple costume of wide-legged hakama pants and tops in brilliant shades of red.  The first movement is a beautiful adagio, in which two dancers lean on and catch each other, moving in deep pliés, dramatic gesture and mesmerizing unison.  The pace reflects the hypnotic quality of the spare, avant-garde score by Kato Hideki and Ana Milosavljevic.

The second movement is set to John Adams “The Chairman Dances” (a precursor to his opera Nixon in China.) The Ensemble enters as well-mannered commuters on a train (Could there be a more iconic image of Japan?), comprised of spotless white chairs.  The dancers go on to carry these chairs across stage in various patterns to conjure different spaces.  In this way, the Ensemble share a group identity –  dispassionate, disciplined and resolute.  At one point the dancers all don identical bright red suit jackets, adding to the drama of their lockstep existence.  One wonders, in the struggle to rebuild, have the many sublimated their identities to the whole, in order to support the unit?  Are they, as it were, empty suits?  And how does the individual survive in this sea of red?  Some do rebel.  Within a rectangle of light, a woman dances vigorously, pushing back at her restrictions to the extent she repeatedly dives off the chairs and into the arms of surrounding ensemble.   Heroes ends with an individual gesture, a final iconic image.  And the beat goes on.

THE COMPANY – Eli Alford, Itzkan Barbosa, Luca De-Poli, Francesca Forcella, Savannah Green, Jared Kelly, Eileen Kim, Lanie Jackson, Mathis Joubert, Skyler Lubin, Jonathan Montepara, Jerard Palazo, Minori Sakita, Ben Schwarz, Ashley Simpson, Peter Weil

Beautiful Once: Choreographer: Jodie Gates, Composer:  Ryan Lott, Lighting Designer: Michael Korsch, Costume Designer: Martha Chamberlain

Macaroni: Choreographer: Loughlan Prior, Composer: Claire Cowan, Lighting Designer: Michael Korsch, Costume Designer: Emma Kingsbury

Heroes, Choreographer: Takehiro Ueyama, Music: Tokoshieni by Kato Hideki and Ana Milosavljevic; The Chairman Dances – by John Adams, Lighting Designers: Christopher Ham & Michael Korsch, Costume Designer:Eugenia P. Stallings

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“You’re never going to believe this.”

This is a perfect show.

Todd Almond, acclaimed performer, songwriter, and playwright is right where he’s supposed to be in this delightfully personal tale. Performed from a piano bench and played out on its accompanying Steinway’s keys, I’m Almost There is a magical mythical musical journey through the mind and all of its distractions, inadequacies, fears, and foibles.

After a “kept me awake all night” impromptu first date walking the city for hours and hours on an Easter Sunday, having a soul-touching conversation that never stopped, Guy (the date) shows up the next day and buzzes Todd’s apartment with two coffees in hand to start the morning and acknowledge the connection that was made the previous day.

With parallels to Homer’s The Odyssey, Todd begins a journey down the stairs of his building to the sidewalk below and is accosted by his neighbor who lost her cat, the physical draw of the gorgeous man next door, succumbs to joining a pyramid-scheme cult by the look-alike sister of the cat lady, knowingly being drawn into the lifestyle and apartment of the buildings vampire, carrying his future-self back up the stairs, and fending off his part mother/part cat in the pits of hell (basement).

These highly imaginative and fantastical plot points showcase the mind of a man who considers himself born “to be on jury duty;” a man both drawn to the flame of love and reticent of the heat that it emits. All of this is deftly sung and told while accompanying himself on the piano, sharing through song, and punctuating dramatic moments with the percussive force that a grand piano can muster.

Accompanying the story and physicalizing several characters on stage is the incredibly talented Erin Hill playing harp as well as contributing on the vocals, and Luke McCrosson playing the bass guitar and piano.

Director David Cromer applies his usual genius  to making the play sing.

Originally commisioned by Audible, you’ve only a couple more chances to see the pitch perfect production of Todd Almond’s I’m Almost There before you’ll have to break down and buy it from Audible.

———-

Audible Theater and Francesca Moody Productions present the New York Premiere of the Audible commissioned musical I’m Almost There. Written and performed by Todd Almond and directed by David Cromer.

Joining Almond on stage are Erin Hill (harp and vocals) and Luke McCrosson (bass).

The creative team includes Jonathan Mastro (music supervisor), David Hyman (costume design), Stacey Derosier (lighting design), Christopher Darbassie (sound design), and Ani Taj (associate director).

Eight performances only Thursday, September 26 – Saturday, October 5 at Audible’s Minetta Lane Theatre (18 Minetta Lane, between MacDougal & 6th Avenue – one block south of W. 3rd Street).

content.rendered:
by Brittany Crowell

Gabriel Kahane was curious.  The political landscape leading up to the 2016 election revealed a different side of America than the bubble he had created for himself.  What was life like outside of Brooklyn?  Was the country as torn and different as it appeared on social media?

What resulted was a 13 day, cross-country trip, taking him from east to west, north to south, and back again via train.  Amongst observation cars and dining cars, he managed to find a delightful cast of characters whose perspectives he imagines as he peppers their stories into his concept album and performance of the same title, “Book of Travelers.”

Running in rep with “Magnificent Bird,” his earlier piece examining his stint away from social media, Kahane’s duo of performances is running at Playwrights Horizons thru October 13.

Kahane is a wonderful performer, his storytelling is engaging, his vocals crisp and beautiful, and his fingers tickle the keys of a piano and guitar so aptly that you feel the songs leaping from the instrument and into the moments he’s encapsulating through music.

The piece is performed in a tight hour and while enjoyable, the narrative doesn’t quite match the depth of Kahane’s musical talents.  The piece felt uneven.  Kahane performed from the bench of a grand piano while surrounded by a dense and exciting environment (scenography by AMP Scenography, Oscar Escobedo).  The speech crafted around the piece’s main focus, the songs of the album, was heavy in the first half and reserved for certain pieces and not others.  

Kahane digs satisfyingly deep into certain characters on the journey, but glosses over others who seem more significant in bringing home the actual thesis of the piece.  While we spend much of the piece discussing a delightful group of Germans, we dig even less deeply into Monica’s story, hearing it only through song without note or context. “What if I Told You” is one of the most moving and thought-provoking songs in the piece, teaching that people are complicated and full of contradictions; it deserved more of a stand-out presence and more discourse than to be slotted between two other songs about passengers along the way.

Part of Kahane’s motivation for the cross-country train ride was a similar ride that his grandmother had taken almost exactly 80 years before.  His final songs of the piece work to understand her place and her journey, not only on the train but also as a part of the American narrative overall.  As he carried her diary with him and brought her along the journey, I hoped we would hear from her more often and that her immigration and emigration played a role in his crafting of the answer to the penultimate question “What is America?” and “Who are Americans?”  As it was, she played a quieter role and there was a missed opportunity in putting her into real conversation with the travelers Kahane met along the way.

“Book of Travelers” is an album of beautifully poetic songs inspired by the sights seen, people met, and personal history explored on one man’s train journey.  That said, the staged presentation lacked a satisfying narrative and failed to reach out and truly grab the heart of this audience member, who was left wondering what was actually discovered on this train and without any big revelations of her own.

 

 

BOOK OF TRAVELERS – Written and performed by Gabriel Kahane

Directed by Annie Tippe

Scenography by AMP Scenography, featuring Oscar Escobedo; costumes by Wendy Yang; lighting design by Chrispoher Bowser; sound design by Garth MacAleavey; production stage manager, Elizabeth Emanuel.  Produced by Playwright Horizons; commissioned by BAM for the 2017 Next Wave Festival.  https://www.playwrightshorizons.org/about/production-history/2020s/2425-season/book-of-travelers-magnificent-bird

title.rendered: Julio Iglesias Jr. at Café Carlyle

content.rendered:
By David Walters

 

Julio Iglesias Jr. and his unique song stylings is debuting live on stage now at Café Carlyle, but only for a short time, October 2-5.

It’s a personal show of sharing some of his most favorite songs. You might be surprised at what they are (Patsy Cline, The Police, Cole Porter), but he makes each one of them his own. Each song choice has a personal meaning that Julio wants to share, and the atmosphere of the café co-conspires with him to make every song an intimate moment with his audience.

Intimacy is only one of the reasons I enjoy going to shows at Café Carlyle.

“New York,” and “elegance,” when you put those words together, shake them in a box and spill them on a table, they spell out Café Carlyle. The Café, in extant since 1955, has had a recent face-lift this past summer, opening up the bar area as well as a few other subtle changes with lighting and decor that makes the intimate room feel lighter. Besides the history and the plethora of talent that has graced its stage through the years, it is a current hot-spot for talent of all genres. With its marvelous music-themed mural walls painted by Marcel Vertès in 1955, cleaned in 2007 from all that cigar smoke from those very fashionable ladies and men in the 50’s and 60’s and 70’s that had darkened much of the murals, distinguished table settings, and elegant staff, the Carlyle is a throwback to the New York of Cary Grant and Audrey Hepburn, to what Gene Kelly, Frank Sinatra, and Jules Munshin sing about in “On The Town.“  However, “the most fabulous sight we can safely say is New York…” not in “the light of the day,” but the dark of the night, and the Cafe Carlyle is one of those sights.

If you’ve never gone, put it on your list of New York things to do. A lovely dinner (cudos to the wait staff), a great show, a fabulous evening.

Julio is flanked by three members of his larger band (as the intimate stage at the the Café is only so big). Camilo Velandia (music arranger) plays both electric and acoustic guitar with a deft alacraty that melds Julio’s voice with the music; Adrian Gines, on drums, box (yes, a wooden box), and percussion adds both bass and air to each song; and Esteban Alberti, normally the sax player, steps up to play both piano and saxophone, sometimes at the same time, creating the wave for the music to ride upon.  The four of them (having played together for quite some time) seamlessly meld music, voice, and words to create a night of sharing love and humor.

—–

Café Carlyle, 35 East 76th Street, New York, New York, 10075

Julio Iglesias Jr. at Café Carlyle, October 1-5   TICKETS

Upcoming shows at Café Carlyle: Rita Wilson Oct 8-12, Rufus Wainwright Oct 15-19, John Pizzarelli Oct 22-Nov 2, Elizabeth Gillis Nov 6-9, The Garfunkels Nov 12-16, M. Ward Nov 21-23, Issac Mizrahi Nov  26-30, Adrienne Warren Dec 3-7, and Peter Cincotti Dec 17-31.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

After his Pulitzer Prize winning play Fat Ham, you might be interested in going to see playwright James Ijames new play Good Bones now playing at The Public Theater, .

Good bones, yes, the play does have that, but it is also at times confusing and plodding and feels like it is covered in construction plastic, still awaiting the final reveal.

Having moved away as soon as she could, Aisha (Susan Kelechi Watson) has come back to the projects neighborhood she grew up in, “The Heat,” having nothing but bad memories of constantly living in fear during her childhood and what she feels it did to her solo-parenting mother. Her goal is to destroy those traumatic memories by transforming the neighborhood, “heal that place.” She is a community project lead in the construction of a sports complex that will both destroy and transform the neighborhood.

Her contractor, Earl (Khris Davis), is transforming the kitchen of an old house in The Heat that Aisha and her husband Travis (Mamoudou Athie) have bought. Earle is also from The Heat but has found a way, “to turn the darkness into light,” and is hurt that one of its own would think that “sweet talking poor people out of their homes is civic good.” Aisha is newly pregnant and the thought of raising her child in the same neighborhood that she grew up in spurs her on in her work to make changes and also find the reconnection to who she once was.

They each have personal ghosts from the past that are manifested in unexplained sounds and movement throughout the house through the course of the play. This is an interesting precept, but only adds to the confusion and murkiness.

“Dangerous places also produce really strong and resilient people,” and that is concretely present in the characters that Mr. Ijames has created. Good Bones is outwardly a play about neighborhood gentrification and is what you will read about in the marketing, but as in all well-constructed plays, it goes deeper and truly finds its strength in the portrayal of the emotional depth of the personal, soul gentrification of the characters involved in the story. That’s what the true reveal of this play firmly rests on.

——–

Good Bones written by James Ijames and directed by Saheem Ali.  

The cast includes: Mamoudou Athie (Travis), Khris Davis (Earl), Téa Guarino (Carmen), and Susan Kelechi Watson (Aisha).

The production includes scenic design by Maruti Evans; costume design by Oana Botez; lighting design by Barbara Samuels; sound design by Fan Zhang; hair, makeup, and wig design by Krystal Balleza; and prop management by Claire M. Kavanah. Darrell Grand Moultrie provides drill choreography for the production and Jack Phillips Moore serves as the dramaturg. Norman Anthony Small is the production stage manager and Giselle Andrea Raphaela is the stage manage

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman 

McNeal, Ayad Akhtar’s new drama which is receiving a star-powered and strikingly staged premiere courtesy of Lincoln Center Theater, is the kind of play where little happens but much is discussed. You may not leave the theater teary-eyed but your brain will be bursting with ideas inspired by this meaty think piece.

Akhtar is interested in the line between reality and fiction, the point where inspiration becomes plagiarism, and the angle of intersection between technology and the plane of human existence. His tools of study are as old as Shakespeare and as new as Artificial Intelligence, as high-minded as a Nobel laureate’s speech and as low-slung as the contemplation of suicide. It’s a heady mix of style and influences, made even more complex by the addition of a metaphysical element that often has the play commenting on itself or suggesting that the whole tale is taking place within the algorithmic whirl of a chatbot app.

The egotistical Jacob McNeal (Robert Downey Jr.) is a wildly successful novelist, a recent Nobel recipient and an alcoholic on the cusp of dying from liver disease. He is also something of a Hamlet. It is not just because he is visited by a ghost and speaks of cradling a skull, but he is also quite consumed over whether to be or not to be. And, having become obsessed with generative A.I., he just might have found a way to have it both ways. Feeding his experiences and influences into the technology not only allows him to create new works instantly, it might just let him live forever, give or take his blood and bones. As he will come to ask by the evening’s poetic end, “Does my heart thrum still in a chest not flesh, but words?”

The play’s supporting characters, six humans and a chatbot, each have a specific duty in the story and are defined by their relation to McNeal as opposed to having fuller lives of their own. It is nearly as if they are A.I. generated plot devices, which is likely the point. Sahra Grewal (Ruthie Ann Miles) is McNeal’s doctor, in charge of reminding him of his mortality and supplying experimental drugs. When he mixes those drugs with liquor, the result is a dark hallucination played out with the same assuredness that a chatbot has when it hallucinates.

Stephie Banic (Andrea Martin) is McNeal’s literary agent in charge of injecting some comedy into the proceedings, though Martin’s physical humor seems forced here, not quite computing with the otherwise sure-handed direction of Bartlett Sher. Dipti (Saisha Talwar) is Banic’s underling but serves primarily as a flirtatious offering to buffer McNeal’s fragile ego. Harlan (Rafi Gavron) is McNeal’s justifiably angry son who arrives pissed off and leaves devastated by family secrets. Natasha (Brittany Bellizeare) is a reporter who tries to crack McNeal open and Francine (Melora Hardin) is a former lover who would prefer he remain a closed book. As for the chatbot, it manifests as a series of text messages projected onto the stage at McNeal’s whim, serving him up his destiny.

In the Iron Man films, Downey Jr. portrayed a superhero whose heart is shielded by experimental technology. In his Broadway debut, he turns in a solid performance in a role that occupies a lot of stage time but requires few heroics. His McNeal is more of a pewter man, possessing a low melting point, a malleable code of ethics and a technology that lives on his iPhone, leaving his heart unprotected.

It seems only fitting that A.I. should have the final word on this production, so here is a conclusion generated by Claude.ai. I couldn’t have said it better myself: “Ultimately, McNeal challenges audiences to grapple with profound questions about creativity, mortality, and the evolving relationship between humans and A.I. While the play’s intellectual ambitions occasionally overshadow its emotional resonance, Akhtar’s thought-provoking script and Downey Jr.’s nuanced performance make for a compelling, if cerebral, theatrical experience.”

 

McNEAL – By Ayad Akhtar; directed by Bartlett Sher.

WITH: Robert Downey Jr. (James McNeal), Ruthie Ann Miles (Sahra Grewal), Andrea Martin (Stephie Banic), Saisha Talwar (Dipti), Rafi Gavron (Harlan McNeal), Brittany Bellizeare (Natasha Brathwaite) and Melora Hardin (Francine Blake).

Sets by Michael Yeargan & Jake Barton, costumes by Jennifer Moeller, lighting by Donald Holder, sound by Justin Ellington & Beth Lake, and projections by Jake Barton. Lincoln Center Theater, the Vivian Beaumont Theater, 150 West 65th St., https://www.lct.org. Through November 24. Running time: 1 hour 40 minutes

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Honor is a very heady play that slanders the inhumanity of the corporate world. It is dense with the workings of corporate culture and the doggedness of its singular vision, self.

It was way back in the 1880s when corporations, with the help of the 14th amendment, became actual people with all the accompanying legal rights and privileges. This has led us to where we are today in that, as head lawyer Ludwig Cade (John Blaylock) makes clear as the company spokesperson, “We don’t serve truth and justice.”

Then what are the guiding principles of companies?  Survival at all costs and avoidance of litigation with a dollar sign or two, or three, as their actual true logo.  What a company then in turn asks of its employees, is to re-calibrate their personal sense of truth and justice and redefine it as the company sees fit.

Honor will leave you disgusted by the world of work and what people turn themselves into for their piece of the pie.

In a conference room at an undisclosed business, HR (Alinca Hamilton) and Legal (John Blaylock) meet to put the closing final touches on a charge levied against an executive employee. The final consensus, after hiring outside counsel to investigate, is that there is no evidence of harassment and intimidation supporting the charge. The accuser has been subsequently bought off with a severance package and dismissed. The only problem, the accused (Ed Altman), wants a public apology from the company and will not stand down until he gets it thus reclaiming his misguided sense of lost honor.

As I said, the script is very left brain dealing with the inconstant nature of truth and honor both for the individual and for the company with it’s accompanying platitudes. The play will demand a lot of you as you are presented with white board presentations of how a company operates. It is very well thought out and the arguments and points of view are played out with a strong conviction and lack of compunction.

What it will not ask of you though is to care. As a company can never truly become a person, despite the 14th amendment, each character, in their roles as employee, are just as hard pressed to care about either.

What is lacking is humanity, and I guess that’s the point.

————

Written and directed by T.J. Elliott, Honor stars Alinca Hamilton, John Blaylock, and Ed Altman. The production team includes Gifford Elliott (technical & artistic director), Marjorie Phillips (costumes), and Kate Gavin (stage manager).

Honor runs until October 6, Wednesday – Saturday at 7pm & Sunday at 1pm. The Gene Frankel Theater is located at 24 Bond Street. Running time is 70 minutes. Tickets are $25 (use code HONOR15 for 15% off), available at www.our.show/honor

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

“Then Trump became President.” If that bit of dialog from early on in Fatherland ties your stomach in knots, prepare to be fully triggered by play’s end. This true story and brutal reminder of recent events captures one family’s trauma when, in and around the January 6, 2021 attack of the U.S. Capitol, a father loses his way down a conspiratorial rabbit hole causing his loving teenage son to turn on him. With breakneck pacing and powerful performances from its two leads, the production rips the bandage off a wounded moment in our history. It’s supposed to hurt less that way, but it doesn’t; the sting lingers long after leaving the theater.

Director Stephen Sachs presents a minimalist staging of a Capitol rioter’s federal trial that took place in early 2022. The accused is a Texan named Guy Reffitt (Ron Bottitta) and the prosecuting attorney’s witness is Guy’s boy (Patrick Keleher) who not only observed his Dad’s growing extremism, but alerted the FBI about it two weeks prior to the Capitol attack. We, the audience, serve as jury while the case is spelled out via testimony and flashbacks. On the face of it, this is a tale of son against father, or the ways of treason against the bulwark of democracy. But the more interesting conflict turns out to be the son’s internal struggle between the guilt over tearing his family apart and the need to protect himself and his kin from a possible madman. 

Also on trial is the script, which is taken verbatim from court evidence, public statements, and the official transcript of the trial. It’s Show v. Tell with perhaps an over-reliance on the tell. Sympathy for the son is almost too easily earned when an attorney (Anna Khaja) can simply ask “How are you feeling?” or, leadingly, “Do you consider your father dangerous?” The technique also asks us to do without some moments that, in a fictional work, would be key. Most notable is the interplay with Guy’s wife. She is frequently discussed; a central character who is never made flesh. Also, a private scene between the prosecutor and the defense attorney (Larry Poindexter) would have been a welcome way of humanizing these characters who struggle to find much depth, though Poindexter’s smirk at the proceedings does offer a flash of wit.

A better balance is achieved in tracking the father’s tumble into militia-land. An oil worker who loses his job and drinks too much, he “needed an outlet, and he found one” in what Donald Trump had to offer. It’s a shockingly short, straight path from quoting The Art of the Deal to joining up with the far-right Three Percenters to obsessing over BLM and Antifa to thinking the Chinese are going to halt the election to driving to D.C. with a car full of ammo.

This production comes to New York from L.A.’s Fountain Theatre giving us the gift of seeing two fine West Coast performers strut their stuff. Bottitta’s portrayal of the father is strikingly menacing while never over the top, though his character’s choices leave little room for sympathy. And as the son, Keleher’s mostly understated performance makes him all the more relatable.

Despite its courtroom setting, Sachs keeps his actors in near constant motion with the son, at one point, literally running in circles even as he is supposedly giving testimony. Scenic designer Joel Daavid gives them plenty of room to roam with a set of just two tables and three chairs. He has also created a strange backdrop that might be an abstract version of the Capitol building, but trying to figure out what he had in mind proved more distracting than informative.

Fatherland is scheduled to run through November 23, giving play-goers the option to see it on either side of the upcoming election. One can choose their own adventure: relive the awful past in the relative calm of October, or take it all in under the full knowledge of whatever lies ahead.

 

Fatherland – Conceived and directed by Stephen Sachs.

WITH:  Ron Bottitta (Father), Patrick Keleher (Son), Anna Khaja (U.S. Attorney) and Larry Poindexter (Defense Attorney).

Scenic Design by Joel Daavid; Lighting Design by Alison Brummer; Sound Design by Stewart Blackwood; and Costume Design by Danyele Thomas. Fountain Theatre at New York City Center Stage II, 131 W. 55th St., nycitycenter.org ,(212) 581-1212. Through Nov. 23. Running time: 80 minutes

content.rendered:
By Victoria L. Dammer

Amanda McBroom: Wintersong

Rest assured that every seat in the theater will be reserved if there is an opportunity to see the talented cabaret singer Amanda McBroom. On September 23, the sold-out audience at Birdland Jazz Club got to experience McBroom’s soon-to-be-released first Christmas album, Wintersong, as the evening’s performance.

Singer-songwriter and actress McBroom, spunky with brownish-red pixie-cut hair and wearing a sparkling black and turquoise jacket, is well known for her Golden Globe-winning tune, The Rose. Bette Midler’s rendition in the movie of the same name made it internationally famous in 1979. No one can deny the continuous energy and draw of McBroom’s career.

The loud applause began with the first song, “Are You Ready,” which, incidentally, was the initial song she wrote with her longtime collaborator, Michele Brourman. The song was comic, setting the tone for the rest of the night as McBroom engaged with her fans, something she appeared quite at ease doing.

Her followers always enjoy her hokey song, “Eggs.” Perhaps this somewhat ease-into-it late-night question couples ask each other after a hook-up occurs more than we know, for everyone in the room loudly applauded. The lines in the song are sexually tactical, asking, “How do you like your eggs?” I can’t deny that I wish I had used that pickup line once or twice in my dating career.

McBroom performed a moving, mournful rendition of Joanie Mitchell’s River, a hauntingly beautiful Christmas-theme song released in 1971. It’s thought to be about Mitchell’s breakup with Graham Nash, and the mix of happiness at Christmastime and the sadness of separation is painful.

McBroom also delighted us with the world debut of the song First Snow of the Year, written by Ken Hirsch and Rosie Casey. This sorrowful song will tug at your heartstrings.

The gifted actress and singer Heather MacRae was a guest star, performing the song Hope Floats, much to the delight of all. MacRae was like a Christmas present, her voice so perfectly wrapped up in the tune.

Another memorable evening treat was bass player Ritt Henn’s song “I Give Up.” His deep voice and skill on the bass exhibited the joyfulness of the crowd.

McBroom wrapped it up with her encore, Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas, a crowd-pleaser. When asked why she made a holiday album, McBroom is quoted as saying, “I am a sucker for Christmas. I have always loved this holiday. The songs return me to my childhood.”

We can celebrate her love for the Christmas season, even in September or any other time of year.

Amanda McBroom: Wintersong at Birdland Jazz Club. Press by Betsyann Faiella.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

In Medea: Re-Versed, actor/rapper/playwright Luis Quintero has developed a unique and incredibly exciting style of storytelling.   In stretching hip hop as an art form beyond its colloquial, contemporary space to illuminate the mythic tale of a woman driven to make a horrifying choice, Quintero has found his own theatrical voice, one that brings drama to life with riveting immediacy.

The production values reflect both the beat and the style.  Bright, colorful lights play over the audience as if we were at an extravaganza, in a black box theater.  It is delicious.  Lights punctuate and dazzle throughout the performance, as action and reaction.  Electric bass (Melissa Mahoney) and guitar (Siena D’Addario) play one irresistible funky groove after another while Mark Martin beatboxes discreetly, in prelude to the start of the show.  And then the proverbial doors fly open and we’re off on a high energy, at times high volume, sound and light journey to an alternate reality.

A classic rap battle complete with men in black zip-up jackets and sunglasses, frames the action.  Stephen Michael Spencer, who also plays hot-headed, scrappy Jason in search of fame and riches, darts low and fast.  Jacob Ming-Trent, who doubles as Kings Creon and Ageus, is more subdued but no less intense.  He does some beautiful work, particularly as a Messenger traumatized by death, news of which he is tasked to convey to Medea.  As rap warriors, these two, as well as Luis Quintero, a polished, intelligent, earnest Emcee, are our Greek chorus.  They speak for us and to us.

But what of Medea?  Oh yes…  Goddess, queen, burning pillar of women’s frustration at the unholy unfairness of a culture that privileges one sex over another, that allows a selfish man to abandon a woman and then punish her for being abandoned – this is Medea.  Married to Jason, she is left in limbo to raise the kids while he is away at sea.  Upon his return what does he do?  Announce he is trading her in for a new model, and by the way he wants to take the children.  And of course, because he’s a man, he’ll get away with it.  Queen though she may be, descended from gods and mortals, and possessing the gift of magic, Medea is nonetheless a second-class citizen to her treacherous husband.  Enter, feminine rage.

One could not find a Medea to burn brighter than Sarin Monae West.  She is magnificent.  She electrifies the stage, drawing a detailed, very human portrait that dares to express sympathy for a woman driven to near madness by betrayal.  Tall, elegant, powerfully expressive yet also delicate and subtle, West is laser focused.  She moves with intention and grace, her vulnerability is as powerful as her fire within.  She prowls, she cries, she whispers, and when she wants to – she can cut you like a knife.

Instead of scorned and vengeful, this Medea has been scorned and seeks revenge.  Her emotions are no mere imprimatur, they are lived experience.  Quintero honors her as a woman and a mother.  He honors her as a person who has been wronged and who refuses to be a victim.  In a grand, gruesome law of unintended consequences, the weaponizing of reproduction against women leaves them with only one means to express power, through their children.  If in murdering her own children also Medea self-immolates, so be it.  She was just a means to an end.  An end she can end, thus ending herself.

Medea Re-Versed is neither a translation, a transliteration nor a modernization — it is sui generis.  Boldly colorful, nuanced and brazen, Quintero pays honor to the allegorical grandeur of the original, while tracing a new visceral path into our hearts.  Medea loses nothing in its “re-versing” – indeed, Quintero has reversed time, opening a wormhole to Ancient Greece, where we feel as the ancients must have felt as the curtain came down on Euripides’ immortal story.  Devastated.  Speechless.  Weeping.

Medea Re-Versed by Luis Quintero, adapted from the Euripides; Co-Conceived & Directed by Nathan Winkelstein.  Featuring: Siena D’Addario, Melissa Mahoney, Mark Martin, Jacob Ming-Trent, Luis Quintero, Stephen Michael Spencer, Sarin Monae West.

Lighting Design by Cha See; Music Director Mark Martin; Sound Design Matt Otto; Scenic Design by Emmie Finckel; Costume Design by Nicole Wee; Movement Director Tiffany Rachelle Stewart.

Presented by Red Bull Theater and Bedlam.  Running through October 13th at The Sheen Center, Frank Shiner Theatre, 18 Bleecker Street, NYC.  For tickets: click HERE or go to www.redbulltheater.com.

Running time 80 minutes with no intermission.  WARNING: STROBE LIGHTS ARE USED IN THIS PRODUCTION.  Note:  The show has some seriously loud moments, so earplugs are available at the ticket booth if you would like.  THERE WILL BE A BRIEF POST SHOW FACILITATION 10-MINUTES AFTER CURTAIN FOR EACH PERFORMANCE

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Victoria Dammer

In the conflicted, chaotic world of present-day religious differences, Pamela Weiler Grayson has written Observant. Three generations of women, each connecting with their Jewish identities, come to grips with their different emotions during a terroristic attack at a local synagogue. This isn’t Israel, as one might think–it’s the quiet suburb of Scarsdale, New York.

Amy (Melissa Wolff) is Jewish, but Christmas is her most fantastic time of the year. There’s no menorah or decorations in the apartment to celebrate Jewish holidays. Instead, she decorated the home with a Christmas tree, and carols filled the air.

She is also planning to celebrate her 60th birthday, having invited her younger daughter Zoe (Arielle Flax) and her boyfriend Farrokh (Fady Demian) home for the weekend. Zoe describes Farrokh as a “cultural Muslim,” admitting they have the same attitudes towards religion as many people; it is either big or small or non-existent. Arriving with their infant son is her older daughter Sarah (Arielle Beth Klein), an observant Jew, and her deeply religious husband Josh (Yair Ben-Dor). They value Jewish tradition, and you can immediately feel the friction in the room.

Tension automatically erupts between the sisters, the mother, and the daughters, coupled with Sarah’s quick militant behavior, which makes everyone feel uncomfortable in her presence. Sarah spews vitriol toward her mom about the lack of Jewish tradition in the house. Her husband takes a softer approach but is still outspoken with his views.

Zoe defends Farrokh, telling Sarah, “Please don’t do this in front of Farrokh,” while he acts graciously about her tone. The audience laughs when he says, “Please don’t feel the need to act differently in front of me,” to which Zoe replies, “They need to.” Sarah’s lack of tolerance for those who differ from her and her husband is alarming for one who claims to be religious.

Multiple loud sirens and the news that a shooting has occurred at a local synagogue interrupt the evening. Amy is in despair as her mother, Nancy (Rebecca Hoodwin), is attending the service with friends. In a state of panic, Amy receives the news that her mother has been shot, quickly rushes to the hospital, and brings her to the apartment. Despite canceling the birthday celebration, the conversation about religion persists without interruption.

Sarah tries to lighten the tone, asking all to join in prayer. She wants them all to take part in Shabbat, to bring “a little bit of joy and light into a really shitty situation.” But does prayer overshadow the impossibility of understanding each other’s views on religion? Can we tolerate this multicultural society when struggling with hatred fueled by the global climate?

Observant will make you rethink your views on religious differences and racism, which hasn’t changed for eons. There is an ongoing struggle, no matter what.

Observant, written by Pamela Weiler Grayson and directed by Shellen Lubin. Starring Melissa Wolff, Arielle Flax, Fady Demian, Arielle Beth Klein, Yarr Ben-Dor, and Rebecca Hoodwin. Press by Andrea Alton/Alton PR. Several actors appear courtesy of the Actors’ Equity Association.

The show runs 1 hour and 40 minutes without interruption through September 28 at The Chain Theatre.

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

The Irish Repertory Theatre sails into their 36th season on a slow boat. Making its American premiere, Nancy Harris’s 2019 drama, The Beacon, takes its time navigating the troubled waters stirred up by a foursome who come together on an island off the coast of West Cork only to realize they are better off apart. As directed by Marc Atkinson Borrull, this voyage is full of pretty views but short on dramatic tension; while the star we are meant to follow (Kate Mulgrew) sometimes dims or vanishes all together.

Mulgrew portrays Beiv, a successful abstract painter living alone in her island cottage. “I’ve nothing to hide,” she declares early on, and as if to prove it she is in the midst of transforming her home into a “glass box” with a wall replaced by windows affording an expansive view of the sea (excellent projection design by Colm McNally). But her art and her circumstances tell another story. Her latest painting, an ominous globular orb, she declares, is simply a blood orange. Others see it as a feminist statement. But by play’s end it will come to represent a pit of despair tied to Beiv’s husband who died a mysterious death some ten years prior. 

Beiv’s son, Colm (Zach Appelman) and his new bride, Bonnie (Ayana Workman), travel from their San Francisco home to spend their honeymoon at the cottage only to find that the guest bedroom has been demolished as part of Beiv’s renovation work. It is an apt metaphor for the couple. To say that the newlyweds are inseparable would be to deny that they are always apart, especially after a spat sends Bonnie out the door for most of the night. But coming in the door is Donal (Sean Bell), a local who is building Beiv’s patio and whose ties to his old chum Colm are deep and complicated. He is not so much surprised to hear that Colm is recently married as he is shocked to learn that he married a woman.

Mulgrew gives a quiet performance for most of Act One, struggling to find an inner life for her guarded character while unconvincingly painting away at a canvas. She is missing in action for a large part of the second act but once she returns, and given meatier material to chew on, she ultimately finds a poignant path to a tearful end and a bond, at last, with her son. Less clear is why she spends much of the play wearing huge eyeglasses that obscure her face while at other times her vision is apparently fine.

As Colm, Appelman tries mightily to balance the emotional weight of a wife who is uninterested in their marriage against a mother and a friend who both want into his heart. Simultaneously, he is busy burying the memory of his father, harboring a fear of boats, being drunkenly randy and giving off vibes of a Silicon Valley dude who is a bit of a snit. Is it any wonder he is a mess by the last scene when he must also muster the energy to finally come to terms with his mother’s anguish?

Workman’s Bonnie is at first an irritant then just generally hard to believe in the actions she takes, including palling around with a scheming podcaster (David Mattar Merten) who wants in on Beiv’s secrets. And as Donal, Bell stealthily steals the show, moving into the center of all the action, stirringly broken-hearted over his true wishes and feelings for Colm.

As perhaps fitting for a work that dwells on a painting, Borrull’s direction favors creating handsome visuals, but it comes at the cost of pacing. Especially deadly is a silent, extended scene of Beiv setting a dinner table just so, which does little to add to our understanding of her. On the upside, the approach allows McNally’s scenic and lighting design to shine with an appropriately chilly glow. 

 

The Beacon – By Nancy Harris; Directed by Marc Atkinson Borrull

With Zach Appelman (Colm), Sean Bell (Donal), David Mattar Merten (Ray), Kate Mulgrew (Beiv) and Ayana Workman (Bonnie).

Set and lighting design by Colm McNally, costume design by Orla Long, sound design by Liam Bellman-Sharpe, properties by Nicole Rozanski. The Irish Repertory Theatre, 132 West 22nd St., 212.727.2737, https://irishrep.org. Through November 3. Running time: 2 hours 30 minutes

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

In The Roommate, a Bronx woman looking to escape her nefarious past heads to Iowa where she rooms with a Midwestern woman living alone after her marriage ends and her son relocates to the big city.  What ensues is a charming and funny romp, as the two women surprise each other and find that the “words” people find for themselves don’t always equate to the sum of our parts.  

[While tempting to provide further plot points, I wouldn’t want to spoil the many quirks and surprises revealed throughout the piece – so I’ll leave it at that!]

Playing at the Booth Theater thru December 15, The Roommate by Jen Silverman is reminiscent of [an updated and more engaging] The Odd Couple; bringing together the perfect pair in Patti LuPone and Mia Farrow.  LuPone embodies a more muted and nuanced role than her typical bold, brash leading lady; playing straight to Farrow’s quirky Midwest, and bringing depth and balance to the piece.  Farrow shines as Midwestern Sharon, doling out endless charm and humor, and endearing the audience to the lost woman who is so desperately looking for connection in her large, empty house surrounded by large, open fields.

Silverman’s piece, coupled with direction from Jack O’Brien, slowly breaks down the two women’s names for themselves as the seemingly vastly different individuals discover their similarities and secrets and build a friendship and understanding with each other.  The Roommate is a piece about who we are and how we see each other, how our perceptions can mislead us, and how honesty and genuineness can lead to wonderful friendships.  O’Brien stages Silverman’s story with subtlety and craft, causing small surprises to jump off the page and wooing audiences to each of the lost ladies.  By the end of the piece the audience feels like a third member in this newly formed friendship.

Bob Crowley’s scenic design (supported by Natasha Katz’s lighting design, Mikaal Sulaiman’s sound design, and David Yazbek’s original music) chooses to epitomize emptiness, featuring a larger-than-life house frame donned with sheer fabric walls, and a massive back screen projecting vast open fields.  Projections also hint at what may be brewing beneath during thundery transitions from evening to morning.  Crowley’s costumes (with hair, wig, and makeup by Robert Pickens & Katie Gell) serve to highlight the disparity between the two women, embodying Bronx and Iowa perfectly, while subtly influencing each other as the piece continues.

The Roommate is surprising, charming, and highly enjoyable with stand-out performances by its star-studded cast and a feel-good story that will have you smiling for the rest of your evening.  Don’t miss it!

THE ROOMMATE – by Jen Silverman; directed by Jack O’Brien

FEATURING: Mia Farrow (Sharon) & Patti LuPone (Robyn)

Scenic and costume design by Bob Crowley; lighting by Natasha Katz; sound by Mikaal Sulaiman; music by David Yazbek; hair, wig, and makeup by Robert Pickens & Katie Gell; movement direction by Simone Sault.  Running at the Booth Theater thru December 15; run time 100 minutes.  https://theroommatebway.com/

content.rendered:
By David Walters

It’s California, up in the mountains. Johnny is dead. Rolled his truck and didn’t survive the crash.

His sister (Alexandra Gellner) and brother (Garrett Richmond) get a couple of pizzas and a keg and get the word out for a party in his honor. Sis sends an invite to Annie Rae (Aimee Fortier) who now lives in New York City, and who ten years ago was his girlfriend for three years, the longest relationship he ever had. Annie Rae got away from where she grew up and is making something of herself in the big city. None of the others can make that claim and harbor animosity and resentment towards her. Annie Rae has guilt from her past for leaving those friends behind and has unfinished internal business that compels her to attend the party, with her boyfriend (Jamie Effros) in tow. Annie Rae had changed her name (to Annette) when she left home and is trying to make a new person out of herself and leave the past behind. Going back she realizes that the people (especially her best friend Elaina (Rachel Griesinger)), the place, and her childhood experiences will always be a part of her no matter the distance.

The Players Theatre, up two flights of stairs at 115 MacDougal Street, is a small blackbox theater seating approximately 25 people. It’s a good place to try out a play, see how it gels, and get a little audience perspective.

The strong point of this production is the great ensemble work by the whole cast. They were able to truthfully portray history with each other, indulging in familiar/familial banter, and insult each other with love in the way that only having spent time with people can. It was believable that they knew each other for a long time and had gone through some life things together. It was a pleasure to see that cohesiveness.

The script, by Kara Ayn Naplitano, is tight, clicks along nicely, and excellently handles the emotional slow reveal of her characters. Honesty and communication were never strong points of any of them, reacting and striking out is what they do first. The great ensemble work could not have been accomplished though without a good script to base it on.

A personal tale of discovery, well told, and expertly acted.

—–

In Search of Elaina was written by Kara Ayn Napolitano and directed by Joy Donze,

With: Rachel Griesinger, Aimée Fortier, Jamie Effros, Alexandra Gellner, Garrett Richmond, Greg Carere, and Lee Tyler.

The production team: Rachel Razor (scenic design), Sasha Lysenko (lighting), Robert Gonyo (sound design), Arielle Legere (stage manager).

In Search of Elaina runs September 5 – 22, Thursdays – Saturdays at 7pm and Sundays at 3pm. The Players Theatre is located at 115 MacDougal Street, New York NY 10012 (accessible from the A,C,E trains at West 4th Street). Please note that the theatre is located on the 3rd floor of a walk up; there is no elevator.

For tickets and more information, visit www.insearchofelaina.com.

I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs
In Vile Isle, currently playing at the Tank, a beautiful Drag Diva prophet of doom presides over chaos as a flood of Biblical proportions threatens  humanity, sending four men on a tempest-tossed voyage to salvation.  As the storm worsens, human fallibility undermines their relationships – and endangers their futures.  The play takes on ‘big picture’ issues almost on the sly.  Addiction, adultery, identity and loyalty weave their way through a narrative whose serious nature is leavened by broad comedy.  Even as it veers from Keystone Cops to Don Giovanni, at its heart Vile Isle is a human story.
Any play could easily falter under the weight of such ambition.  Nevertheless, Vile Isle totally works.  It works because author Justin Halle has written a farce with legs.  It works because Spencer Whale has directed the action in a clean and crisp manner, balancing high comedy and Greek Tragedy.   It works because the actors approach their characters seriously.   Actors who play for stakes take you with them even if the journey veers deeply into the absurd.
Nathan (Sam Gonzalez), is drama central – the queen of clever ripostes, and dramatic exits.  Gonzalez tosses off one-liners with just enough snark.  His boyfriend, the earnest, suit-clad Alex (Kenon Veno) is charmingly uncool.  He is a late bloomer when it comes to being out as a gay man.  Similarly new to the game, Christopher (Max Kantor) a devoted, if somewhat dim, D.J. is anxious to prove his gay cred.  Kantor bounds through their lines with almost boyish intensity – a man without a country, as it were, in search of a passport to his identity.  Up to now, that identity has been wrapped up in his relationship with Ziz (Julian Socha) whose vulnerability anchors the narrative.  Ziz is our way in, as it were.
The motivating factor in this disco dramedy is Lizzie Fine (Mariyea Jackson).  Lanky, beautiful and funny, Lizzie drives the action even as she is equally endangered by the storm.  Lizzie is doing her best to corral people onto an ark of her own design – which will be a safe haven for gay and queer people.  She is doing her best to preserve this group who have endured scorn, plague, mistreatment and abandonment.  She is so DONE with that.  Whether exasperated or commanding, Mariyea takes stage like the diva she is.  All heads turn.  With each entrance, Lizzie arrives more layered – literally – in narrative.  David Hyman‘s wildly idiosyncratic costume design piles denim upon beads, upon lame, eventually topped by a slicker – even a miner’s lamp and a wisp of police tape, as she grows more and more burdened by what she is going through offstage.
Everything about Vile Isle is inventive.  Dan Daly‘s set design of Alex’s apartment perfectly evokes a modern vibe with chic 60s furniture in mustards and aquas that immediately convey that Alex has impeccable taste (and money).  The production design makes a virtue of necessity, given the small space at the Tank.  Indeed, the insular space serves the narrative effectively.  Even when the ark barges in (no pun intended), clumsy gangplank and drooping glittery garlands in tow, we somehow still feel there is an ‘outside.’  Yichen Zhou‘s lighting follows suit, from fabulous DJ glam party to moody storm.  The only issue I have with the production is it’s a bit loud.  Between the Dance music of the pre-show and the intense dialogue over hot mics, the volume begins to overwhelm.
In quirky plot points, dramatic speech, tumultuous activity and fast paced dialogue (and a few surprises), Vile Isle tells many stories at once.  One of my favorite moments is a strobe-lit scene worthy of silent film, incorporating a key set change as the flickering light suspends both time and place.  With this device, director Spencer Whale cleverly pauses the action by incorporating lots of action.  Indeed, the play traffics in contrasts and contradictions.  It is unexpectedly moving, as the four men face their day of reckoning and rediscover the sweetness of friendship.  The wages of sin may be high, but forgiveness is a bargain at twice the price.
Vile Isle, written by Justin Halle, directed by Spencer Whale.  With Sam Gonzalez, Kenon Veno, Julian Socha, Max Kantor and Mariyea Jackson.
Scenic Design by Dan Daly; lighting design by Yichen Zhou; costume design by David Hyman; sound design by Angela Baughman; video design by Jesse Itskowitz; original music composed by Tralen Doler.
Co-produced by Most Unwanted and the Tank.  Appearing at the Tank (312 West 36th St.) through October 6th..  For tickets go to www.thetanknyc.org  Running time 90 minutes with no intermission.  Please note strobe lighting is used in this production.

In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. title.rendered: “A Fairly Odd Musical” The unauthorized parody

content.rendered:
By Eryn Malafronte

Having been born in 1991 and babysat by the likes of Catdog, Angry beavers, and AH! Real Monsters, as well as being a puppeteer and puppet fanatic; I was eagerly awaiting being brought back to the simpler time of my Saturday morning cartoon days. 

A Fairly Odd Musical- written and directed by Brayden Martino was “ A result of seven years of collaboration by Gen Z artists who want to create the art they long to see in the world”, as Martino himself stated in his creator notes. A truer statement could not have been made about the cartoon fever dream world we were about to enter. 

The show itself is centered around Timmy Turner (CALLAHAN GILLISPIE) and his funny, fantastical, and delightfully foul FairyGodparents, Cosmo and Wanda ( ARTHUR KNOX, TESS GILMORE), trying to overthrow the brand new mega streaming network Dimma + created by Doug Dimmadome (LUCAS BONIFACE). This challenge proves to be a taller order than Dimmadome’s iconic hat. Dimma + has proven to be full of unwanted Reboots of our once loved animated shows and movies, and the children of Dimmsdale won’t stand for it! This prompts our fairy Godparents to craft some magic remotes (Nod to an episode of The Fairly Oddparents) to go into the streaming platform themselves and get those unwanted reboots canceled. I will state that although this is a parody of a popular children’s show in the 90’s, this is FAR from a family show, leave the kids at home. There is explicit language and talk of sex and occasional violence- albeit all in good fun! There is also a voting system incorporated in the show as “pop quizzes” for audience interaction, this added a very fun element which is done right from your phone. These “pop quizzes” ranged from the audience reminiscing about some of their own sexual awakenings with their favorite cartoons, or deciphering the best dare for Timmy’s crackpot teacher Crocker (CLAY WEBB) to perform on stage.

A standout in the show for myself was the ensemble.  Mr. and Mrs Turner (NICK ADAM HUMPHRIES, RHEA BRADLEY) particularly had me in stitches, and the vocal/ character work from actors such as Boniface doubling as Dimmadome/a surprise antagonist, Humphries doubling as characters Mr. Turner/ Chet Ubetcha, Webb doubling as Crocker/ Carl Wheezer/ others, and lastly Bradley who doubled as Mrs turner/ Danny Phantom/others; was hilariously refreshing. Callahan herself had a standout vocal performance as Timmy Turner, Chip Skylark (RANDY FORD) also had a standout vocal performance to match the ego of his character. And Trixie (EMILY BANG) delivered a very sweet performance as the sought after love interest of Timmy Turner.

The drawback of the show unfortunately for me lies in the puppetry first and foremost, and some self indulging improv gone on a little too long. As well as utilization of one the shows Iconic characters, Vicky (MELIA JOST) who was only in the show to speak briefly. I think Puppetry can be such a beautiful addition to any show if done properly, it allows the audience to buy into the fantasy without hesitation. If not done properly puppetry can act as a major hindrance and distraction to both the audience as well as actors on stage. These puppets were not appendages of the actors, but more like forgotten phantom limbs. Actors talking to the Godparents on stage were hardly looking at the puppets, and the puppeteers themselves would forget to open their mouths at quite a few speaking moments of the show, it was disappointing to see that so much time and creativity were put into this show and as a puppeteer I feel that puppetry is where they fell short. Seams, hands, and foam could all be seen on, and in the puppets when being operated. It was apparent there was not a lot of confidence in the puppetry and it led to a very distracting performance given one third of the time the audience member wanted to look at the puppet, since that was the character who was supposed to be emoting, but they end up looking at the actor…who is looking at the puppet hoping they opened the mouth on the right syllable. Many times the puppet would be forgotten and upstage itself. As a professional puppeteer it was difficult to digest, especially given the hard work put into the other aspects of this original parody.

That being said it is a very fun show worth seeing! I have high hopes that with the shows continued run they put more thought and care into the puppetry. I believe it would only enhance the creative and hilarious talent that is the See Humans Company and this wonderful show and cast in particular.

The Fairly Odd Musical with Callahan Gillispie (Timmy Turner), Arthur Knox (Cosmo), Tess Gilmore (Wanda), Clay Webb (Crocker), Emily Bang (Trixie), Lucas Boniface (Doug Dimmadome),Randie Ford (Chip Skylark), Rhea Bradley (Mrs Turner), Nick Adam Humprhies (Mr. Turner) Melia Jost (Swing).

Directed, written and produced by Brayden Martino, Composer/ Lyricist Hudson Keown, Choreography by Emma Eileen Hansen, Music Direction by John- William Gambrell, Scenic design Molly Brodowski, Lighting design by Gabe Seplow, Puppet design Tristen Martino, Kenzi Brush.

A Fairly Odd Musicals run time is 2 hours plus intermission, and can be seen at the Jerry Orbach Theater,  starting September 25th every Wednesday at 8pm through December.

Tickets can be purchased at ticket master starting at $67.50, and can be purchased here

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

See What I Wanna See playing now at 154 Christopher Street is an out-of-the-box production by Out of the Box Theatrics.  This remount of Michael John LaChiusa’s 2005 Off-Broadway hit leans into the source material for the piece, three stories by Ryūnosuke Akutagawa, an early 20th century Japanese poet, pulling from Bunraku puppetry styling; translating the initial prelude into Japanese; and bringing together an all-Asian cast to tell the story.

The majority of the choices to highlight the stylings and origin of the source material are successful.  The performance of the puppetry throughout the piece is beautiful with the moments of bunraku being particularly well-crafted and emotionally moving (designed by Tom Lee and led by Justin Otaki Perkins with Nikki Calonge and Takemi Kitamuta).  The translation of the initial song into Japanese was a nice touch as well, although without subtitles it’s a jarring entry to the piece for those less familiar with it, and we lose the detail of the differing perspectives between the first act’s prelude and the second.

The cast is incredibly strong, each showcasing a diverse range between the first and the second act and shining in moments of vulnerability and passion.  Kelvin Moon Loh transforms seamlessly between the uptight and honor driven husband in act one and a lost and manic CPA in act two; Marina Kondo shifts easily between the wife and a ditsy early 2000s down-on-her-luck actress who is just beginning to hope; Sam Simahk is a charming, yet terrifying thief full of life and laughter in act one, becoming an uninspired and quick-to-run reporter in act two; and Ann Sanders who plays a brash and street-smart medium in act one brings a more muted brashness to the dying aunt in act two.  Zachary Noah Piser truly shines as the playful and charming priest in act two: setting up his religious confidence game and then viscerally experiencing what it gives to the hopeless and what it feels like to be a lonely believer; differing from his act one performance as a spritely and pushy janitor at the movie house who discovered the body.

Director, Emilio Ramos leads the team through these transitions of form, style, and character seamlessly, setting the stage for each act and prelude with clarity of time and place and weaving the three different stories together with puppetry, choreography (Paul McGill) and theatricality.  Ramos’ work is supported by Emmie Finckel’s scenic design, Siena Zoe Allen’s costumes, and Kat C. Zhou’s lighting, which set the scene under a bridge archway in central pack, creating a veritable playground for the murder mystery and a proscenium frame for the shadow-play.

See What I Wanna See by Out of the Box Theatrics is a well-crafted, beautifully and emotionally performed revival which breathes new and revitalized life into a 20 year old piece: the first act is an enjoyable murder mystery where conflicting stories question who may to be at blame; the second act, written in the aftermath and processing of 9/11, focuses on religion, faith, and belief. The piece as a whole begs the question: what do we choose to believe and which narratives do we listen to?  Something I’m asking myself quite a bit these days.

For an enjoyable night at the theater with fabulous performances that will give a little something for your brain to nibble on – head to 154 Christopher!

 

SEE WHAT I WANNA SEE – words and music by Michael John La Chiusa; directed by Emilio Ramos; music direction by Adam Rothenberg; choreography by Paul McGill

FEATURING: Aaron J. Albano; Bebe Browning; Nikki Calonge; Takemi Kitamura; Marina Kondo; Kelvin Moon Loh; Justin Otaki Perkins; Zachary Noah Piser; Ann Sanders; and Sam Simahk

Scenic design by Emmie Finkel; costumes by Siena Zoë Allen; puppetry by Tom Lee; sound by German Martinez; lighting by Kat C. Zhou; props by Samantha Shoffner.  Produced by Out of the Box Theatrics: Liz Fleming, founding producing artistic director; Sajari Hume, technical production manager, Lindsay Fuori, operations manager.  Run time: 2 hours, 15 minutes with intermission.  Running at 154 Christopher Street thru September 30.  https://www.ootbtheatrics.com

content.rendered:
By David Walters

This was my second time seeing Our Class. It was reviewed on The Front Row Center in its Under the Radar presentation at BAM in January of this year.

It is being revived at Classic Stage Company in a much smaller space then when it ran at BAM, but what it lost in size, it more than gained in up-close-and-personal, confronting the audience head-on in its questions and pain.

The story (the true tale of what happened to ten members of a school class of five-year-olds, five Catholic and five Jewish, in a small village in Poland beginning in 1925 through to the last one dying in 2003) and its subject matter are emotionally disturbing and the audience is repeatedly challenged with the question”But what could I do?” beginning with the toddlers first response to aggression. This question travels throughout their lives as Poland is taken over first by Communist Russia and then by 221

Nazi Germany. What history tells us is that prior to the Holocaust there were 3.3 million Jews in Poland, and now, maybe a few thousand (depending on how Jewish identity is defined).

But this is not a Jewish play. This is a play, told in lessons, about our world, both present and past, using this story to illustrate our repetitive insanity in inflicting man’s inhumanity to man. The same story is and has been played out over and over again in every country on earth.

At this point in the productions journey the dynamite cast is comfortable and settled with their character’s journey and how they interact with each other, so much so that there is a sense of true play between them. This familiarity has cemented the relationships which makes the cracks in the character’s stories, when they do occur, that much more prominent.

Director Igor Golyak has created a visually masterful production with his staging and adapted Our Class well to the Classic Stage space intensifying the themes and action. The set design (a stage to fly-space chalk board) by Jan Pappelbaum is stupendous and gives the actors and the play the ability to quickly create location and comment on the action, and then just as quickly erased in the very next moment. The projections (period film footage and live video) compliment and add historical context to the plays overarching themes.

Reflecting back from when I first saw this play at BAM, it is still as powerful, still as poigniant, still as relevant, and although the subject matter is dark, will hit you in the gut and make you question humanity. The revived Our Class, in its new space, is still a play that you should make a point to experience.

—

Our Class directed by Igor Golyak, written by Tadeusz Slobodzianek, and adapted by Norman Allen.

With: Gus Barney, Andrey Burkovskiy, Jose Espinosa, Tess Goldwyn, Will Manning, Stephen Ochsen, Alexandra Silber, Richard Topol, Ilia Volok, and Elan Zafir.

Creative Team: Scenic Design by Jan Pappelbaum, Costume Design by Sasha Ageeva, Lighting Design by Adam Silverman, Sound Design by Ben Williams Music, Composed by Anna Drubich, Music Direction by Lisa Gutkin, Projections Design by Eric Dunlap, Chalk Drawings Design by Andreea Mincic, Choreography by Or Schraiber, Hair & Makeup Design by Timur Sadykov, Intimacy & Violence Design by Leana Gardella

Running time is 2 hours and 50 minutes including one intermission.

Tickets can be bought HERE.

Our Class contains material for adult audiences and mature themes. The production includes acts of violence, sexual assault, and antisemitic language, as well as the use of theatrical smoke and haze, and gunshots.

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

Ximena Garnica, one of the creators of A Meal at HERE, gave a brief speech at the end of the show, bidding us goodnight and hoping we would consider the show memorable. They were absolutely indifferent to whether we liked it or hated it. They just wanted it to be memorable. I can say with certainty that it was memorable—as a masterpiece in contradiction. 

For a show that claimed to be about ritual and food—diving into our habits and bringing them to light and making us think about them differently—it simply painted food in the worst possible light. It didn’t make me question or think or hope for something different, it just made me feel disgusted. The show seemed to want us to esteem the rituals surrounding eating throughout different cultures and yet disparaged food constantly. Maybe the contradiction between the two was the point. If explored, that contradiction could have been fascinating. Alas, it wasn’t explored. 

Let me add a huge warning—if you struggle AT ALL with disordered eating of any kind, stay FAR away from this show.

The show showed the most despicable version of food, painting it as something bad and unattractive and even, somehow, unnatural. They showed us every revolting part of eating— bathing vegetables in muddy water, hanging slabs of meat from a line on the ceiling, on and on. Food was abused in so many ways. 

But the beginning was so beautiful! We walked in on a tea ceremony. The actors slowly washed our hands in water. They hung little lantern-like cups of tea around our necks. They wandered slowly among us. Two of the actors stood around a cart in the middle, decked in splendid robes, pouring boiling water in and out of the pot, showing us the way they made the tea and chanting the names of the ingredients in the tea. They lifted their cups of tea in a toast, and we lifted our cups to them, and together we drank. 

After, they took the audience downstairs. We walked by screens depicting nauseating images of food: chewed and mashed. There were strange sounds and creatures dancing and moving. Downstairs, in the theater, they served food; the audience partook in it: that was the whole point of the show, after all. But in structuring the show in that manner, it just felt like they were making fun of the audience— showing how awful the process of making food was and how willing the audience was to eat it. That could have been an interesting approach if it taught the audience something. Unfortunately, instead, it simply felt like the performers were trying to make the audience feel disgusted without conveying fact or information, without conveying any way of doing anything about those feelings of disgust. What’s the point of emotion without action? 

No one ever mentioned the process of food production: what was wrong, what could change. The show seemed to portray food itself as the problem—which was such an invasive claim that I forgot every ACTUAL problem with the food industry I had ever thought about. We can talk about problems with the process of creating, collecting, or serving food but how can we disparage food itself? 

I wish I had learned more from the show. I wish they had depicted more of the Japanese and Colombian heritage that weaved through the show. I wish I had learned more about the details of individual rituals or cultural traditions or food gathering techniques. I think the show missed a huge opportunity to educate. 

There were many stunning parts and wonderful ideas, but it just felt like no one had a clear idea of what they wanted the show to be. For a show with so much potential, so much beauty and purpose carved into it, it fell flat for me, like a beautiful but wildly over spiced dish. 

 

Tickets, which start at $50, can be purchased by visiting www.here.org. The show is running through September 29th.

Ximena Garnica and Shige Moriya are a Colombian and Japanese multidisciplinary artist duo. Their collaborative works manifest as live installations, dance and theater performances, operas, and sculptures that are presented in theaters, museums, galleries, and public spaces. For A Meal, Ximena and Shige bring together new and long-time collaborators to their LEIMAY Ensemble, alongside guest collaborators, performers, composers, and vocalists. These include Masanori Asahara, Krystel Copper, Derek DiMartini, Mar Galeano, Peggy Gould, David Guzman, Dayeon Jeong, Maitlin Jordan, Akane Little, Thea Little, Juan Merchan, Denisa Musilova, Synead Cidney Nichols, Polina Porras, Carolina Oliveros, Irena Romendik, Jeremy D. Slater, Drew Sensue-Weinstein, and Benja Thompson.

title.rendered: Theatre Will Not Prepare You For Death

content.rendered:
By David Walters

I was intrigued about attending Theatre Will Not Prepare You For Death as the title grabbed me and opened my mind to many possibilities. I was further pulled in when I looked at the background of the creative staff and what they were bringing to the piece, the teaser about the theme, the incorporation of dance, and the added vocalizations.

I’m sorry to say I was gravely disappointed at the end of the evening.

The play lacked focus in the acting (pick up your cues), the script (it sounds like a translation), and the (disjointed) directing. Although I could follow the story, it took great effort to pull it out of the weeds of how it was presented and I found myself fighting to stay connected to all the unconnected ideas and concepts. There’s something here to be mined, but not down this tunnel.

The story: A family (mom, dad, two children) return home from burying mom’s mother to find her sitting at the kitchen table eating rice. Theorizing that she has lost her way to get to the other side, they determine that spending time reading Bardo Thodol: The Tibetan Book of the Dead to her would facilitate her crossing, get her unstuck and into the other world. The concept of reading the book is that the person confronts deities, beautiful and terrifying, which are inner projections and then becomes free of this world and is able to move on.

Grandma did not confront any of her inner demons and they became flies buzzing about that came in through the open screen door. After the book was finished, the line, “Well, that didn’t work,” became for me, “Then why did you bother?” What did occur through this process was each family member individually self-reflects and comes to the conclusion that it’s them and their guilt that has caused grandma to not go and each has their private reveal moment hoping that would open the door for her to go through the euphemistic door. We could have had that without the book if that’s the point, and the son’s statement, “Maybe we’re all dead and we just made life up” seemed to ring the truest.

I’m not saying there’s nothing here, as there are some cool concepts and ideas. Especially when the deities are five, mostly unseen by the characters, dancers in Tibetan masks that twist, slither, and slide throughout the space and among the actors creating a mysticalness to the piece. The dancers are a welcome relief. Theatre Will Not Prepare You For Death is billed as an experimental theater piece exploring death, love and family. It’s still in that experimental stage as what’s missing is a cohesive presentation connecting the characters to all of the ideas and concepts.

—-

Theatre Will Not Prepare You For Death is written by Nika Velt and directed by Olga Lvoff and Elena Che.

The actors are Efi Kitsanta, Basil Lvoff, Madeline Naylor, Noah Lang and Kat Shepherd.

Dancers are Kelly Milone, Truth Colon, Liana Zhen-ai and Xavier Townsend.

Throat singer is Deniz Erzaim.

Choreographer is Marla Phelan.

Support comes from The Drilling Company, Lubimovka Play Festival and Positive Exposure.

Presented by Diplodocus Arts at La MaMa Shares, 74 East Fourth Street (La MaMa Shares rents theater space for non-curated productions).
