content.rendered:
By David Walters

Don’t read any further. Stop what you’re doing and get your tickets HERE for what only live theater is capable of, and hurry as it only runs through September 22.

Suspended reality, time travel with the flip of a sign, location and atmosphere created with sound, music, and light, these are things that can only be experienced in a live theatrical forum. If that is something you enjoy and love to participate in, then I’ve got a show for you, Counting and Cracking, now playing at NYU Skirball.

Get tickets HERE.

The Public Theater, in collaboration with Belvoir St. Theatre (Sydney), is showcasing the epic multilingual play Counting and Cracking. It was written by S. Shakthidharan with a masterful blend of depth and levity. It is directed with an often brilliantly ever-flowing dramatic touch by Eamon Flack. This expansive, episodic drama features nineteen performers from six countries playing 50 different characters presenting the play in English, Tamil, and Sinhalese, tracing the multi-generational saga of a Sri Lankan-Australian family from 1956 to 2004.

Get tickets HERE.

Radha escapes Sri Lanka for Australia with her unborn child amidst national turmoil. Two decades on, her son Siddhartha, an Australian unaware of his heritage, receives a transformative call from the past, challenging his identity and beliefs. Counting and Cracking is a celebratory, grand narrative of kinship, reconciliation, the echoes of our past, and the enduring strength of love. A beautiful story of family, home, and self-discovery told in three hours and thirty minutes, with two intermissions, that couldn’t have been told any shorter.

I beg you, do not be frightened by the running time of this show as you will be enthralled and stuck to your seat, incapable of moving, wishing the story and actors would continue long after the final bow.

And I also beg you (as if you can’t tell) to get a ticket HERE to an event that will touch you now and for years to come.

———-

Belvoir St. Theatre of Sydney, Australia, in partnership with The Public, presents Counting and Cracking, by S. Shakthidharan and directed by Eamon Flack.

The cast includes: Rodney Afif, Prakash Belawadi, Senuri Chandrani, Antonythasan Jesuthasan, Nadie Kammallaweera, Ahilan Karunaharan, Abbie-Lee Lewis, Gandhi MacIntyre, Radhika Mudaliyar, Shiv Palekar, Dushan Philips, Sukhbir Singh Walia (Sunny), Nipuni Sharada, Kaivalya Suvarna, Rajan Velu, and Sukania Venugopal. They will be joined by musicians Kranthi Kiran Mudigonda, Janakan Suthanthiraraj, and Venkhatesh Sritharan.

Set and costume design by Dale Ferguson, lighting design by Damien Cooper, and music composition and sound design by Stefan Gregory. Anandavalli serves as choreographer, costume and cultural advisor.

Run time: approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes including two intermissions.

This production contains the use of theatrical haze and smoking on stage.

Will run through Sunday, September 22.

title.rendered: Mahler’s Musical Legacy: An In-Depth Interview with Maestro David Bernard on the ‘Beginnings and Endings’ Mahler Festival

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

NEW YORK – Mahler’s Musical Legacy: An In-Depth Interview with Maestro David Bernard on the ‘Beginnings and Endings’ Mahler Festival

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony (PACS) is one of New York City’s acclaimed classical ensembles, offering artistic brilliance and innovation. Led by the passionate and dynamic conductor David Bernard, PACS has long been known for its impeccable performances and recordings of classical masterworks. Similarly, Maestro Bernard leads the Massapequa Philharmonic Orchestra, Long Island’s premiere orchestra.

What also sets the PACS apart is its unique and groundbreaking approach to audience engagement through its InsideOut Concerts®. In this venue, audience members sit among the orchestra’s musicians, enveloped by the instruments’ sounds, while experiencing the music’s power on a visceral level. This groundbreaking concept erases the boundary between audience and performer, creating an intimate and immediate connection to music often elusive in traditional concert settings.

Conductor David Bernard interacts with audience members in an InsideOut Concert by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

I recently discovered the exciting 2024-25 season program in which the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and the Massapequa Philharmonic Orchestra successively perform Mahler’s 1st and 9th symphonies. I contacted Maestro Bernard for insights into what will be an exhilarating, astounding set of concerts.

Exclusive Interview

In an exclusive interview, we delved deeply into the upcoming Mahler Festival, “Beginnings and Endings,” with Maestro David Bernard, Music Director of the Massapequa Philharmonic and Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. This innovative Festival features performances of Mahler’s First and Ninth Symphonies across the two orchestras in October and November, aiming to provide audiences with a unique experiential gateway into Mahler’s symphonic journey.

Mahler Festival

Edward Kliszus: Thank you for joining me today. Let’s start with a fundamental question: Why do we need a Mahler Festival, and what does it bring to audiences?

David Bernard: Mahler’s Symphonies are monumental in scale and emotional depth and can be intimidating and challenging for newcomers and experienced listeners. The onramp to appreciating Mahler is a daunting commitment, yet for those who take the plunge, Mahler’s music is life-changing. I created this Festival as a gateway for audiences of all levels of sophistication to experience the symphonies of Gustav Mahler on a deeper, more holistic level in an approachable way. By presenting the First and Ninth Symphonies together in a festival, we offer a panoramic view of Mahler’s artistic journey and an opportunity to experience the evolution of his musical language and philosophical outlook in a concentrated and approachable format.

David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony recording of Beethoven and Mahler.

EK: You mention that interpreting and performing Mahler’s works can be challenging. Would you please elaborate on what makes his musical compositions difficult?

DB: Absolutely. Mahler’s symphonies are big, complex, and emotionally challenging works. As I like to say, Mahler puts you directly inside his head, and you see, feel, and experience his inner thoughts and feelings with a realism that is both exhilarating and, at times, overwhelming. It’s as close to an emotional roller coaster as you can get through music. At over an hour of intense musical expression, each symphony requires a significant commitment from the musicians, the audience, and the conductor. The investment required is so substantial that initially, orchestras were reluctant to feature these works frequently or even at all. The cost and effort to produce these concerts were high, coupled with an audience that initially lacked the desire to commit.

David Bernard conducting the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. Courtesy of the Massapequa Philharmonic

The First Live Mahler Cycle (1945)

EK: Given these challenges, how did Mahler achieve the cult following he has today?

DB: This is a fascinating story. The transformation of Mahler’s Symphonies from rarely performed and barely known to be broadly known and loved can be credited to one man—Leonard Bernstein. The rise in popularity of Mahler’s symphonies directly paralleled Lenny’s meteoric rise as a conductor. Bernstein made Mahler a focal point of his work with the New York Philharmonic. From his debut performance of Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 in 1945 at the age of 27 to leading the first live Mahler Cycle performed in the United States to the first high-quality complete set of the symphonies, Lenny was wholly obsessed with Mahler’s symphonies. He was determined to perform them at a time when few conductors, orchestras, and audiences were willing to invest in them. Through his sheer will, he transformed the music world to mirror his obsession. It’s a remarkable demonstration of how one’s love of music if approached with commitment and sincerity, can inspire the world.

EK: Leonard Bernstein was also quite an educator, intellectual, composer, performer, and conductor. Did you know him?

DB: I worked with Lenny at Tanglewood and The Curtis Institute as a student, experiencing his knowledge and generous soul. In contrast to many well-known conductors, Lenny would take the time to engage with students—he was always teaching.

EK: That’s marvelous! You are fortunate to have experienced such an extraordinary association with Bernstein. How did this side of Leonard Bernstein factor into his approach toward popularizing Mahler?

Leonard Bernstein (1955). Photo by Al Ravenna

Four Ways to Say Farewell

DB: Lenny used his passion as a teacher to broaden Mahler’s reach. In 1960, he dedicated an entire Young Person’s Concert to answering “Who is Gustav Mahler?” making Mahler’s complex music accessible to children. However, his extraordinary lecture “Four Ways to Say Farewell,” delving into his interpretation of Mahler’s Ninth Symphony, had the most significant impact. He saw each symphony movement as expressing farewell to this world differently: the first to human love and passion, the second to country life, the third to urban society, and the finale as a farewell to life itself.

EK: That is a beautiful backstory to a symphonic work. Is this a universally accepted view, and do you see it that way?

DB: As much as Lenny and his commitment to Mahler inspire me, I am not convinced by “Four Ways to Say Farewell.” The work of Mahler’s Ninth itself contradicts Lenny’s romanticized view. Composing a symphony on the scale of Mahler’s Ninth requires a “life force” that is not only extraordinarily powerful but also overflowing with optimism and investment in this world. A composer resigned to imminent death couldn’t write a symphony like this.

EK: But Mahler died shortly after writing the Ninth Symphony.

The Composer’s Legacy

DB: Yes, but there’s more to the story. It turns out that following the completion of the Ninth Symphony, Mahler moved to New York and took on the position of Music Director of the New York Philharmonic, so it is a stretch to say he was packing his bags for the other world. It is expected that works written close to a composer’s death are imbued with overly dramatic narratives developed by their survivors who serve the composer’s legacy. Other examples include Mozart’s exquisite Requiem and Tchaikovsky’s Pathétique Symphony.

Mozart took the commission for the Requiem from a Count intending to pass off the work as his own in memory of his wife’s passing. Mozart intended to use this piece as a “job application” to apply for a Church job but died before completing it. It was his death during the composition of the Requiem that triggered the mythology that includes Mozart having written the piece himself as his own Requiem, and of course, the “Amadeus” story where Salieri commissioned it to pass off as his own.

Recursive Classics – David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. Tchaikovsky Symphonies No. 4, 5 & 6 – RC4789671

Tchaikovsky’s death nine days after the premiere of the Pathétique triggered the mythology of “Symphony as a Suicide Note,” but similar to Mahler’s Ninth, the work is so blindingly spectacular that it defies the notion its composer had one foot in the astral plane. Interestingly enough, Mahler’s Ninth and Tchaikovsky’s Pathétique share much more in common than their external mythologies.

EK: How so?

DB: Both Tchaikovsky and Mahler, when they wrote their final symphonies, had reached the pinnacle of their skill in realizing their artistic visions. These works aren’t farewells to life or suicide notes but showcases of their skill, with each movement dedicated to perfecting specific facets of their music that they had focused on intently throughout their careers.

EK: How does this play out in Tchaikovsky’s Pathétique?

The Pathétique

DB: In the Pathétique, each movement represents Tchaikovsky at his finest, but reimagined and freed from societal constraints. The first movement, for instance, is a brilliant reconception of his Romeo and Juliet Fantasy Overture. While Romeo and Juliet took ten years and three versions to reach its final version, Tchaikovsky reportedly composed the first movement of the Pathétique in just three days, with an intensity born from true inspiration.

The second movement transforms Tchaikovsky’s trademark ballet waltz into something new, using a 5/4 time signature that creates a unique, gliding feel. The third movement reinvents his typical symphonic finales with unceasing energy and excitement.

EK: And how does the finale fit into this pattern?

DB: The finale brings us to Tchaikovsky’s present – not as a “suicide note,” as some have claimed, but as a projection of his creative brilliance. Yes, there’s a sense of wistfulness, perhaps acknowledging his mortality, but it’s balanced by the vitality of a composer at the height of his powers.

Photo of Gustav Mahler by Moritz Nähr. Public Domain

EK: How does this relate to Mahler’s Ninth Symphony?

DB: Like Tchaikovsky in the Pathétique, Mahler refined and reimagined vital elements of his compositional style in his Ninth Symphony. The first movement echoes his First Symphony but with greater complexity and self-awareness. It’s as if Mahler is looking back at his younger self with the wisdom of experience, perfecting his approach to symphonic first movements. The second movement is Mahler’s ultimate statement on dance forms – Ländlers and waltzes – which appear throughout his symphonies but reach their zenith here. The third movement showcases Mahler’s “Grand Style” – an intricate, transparent counterpoint that he’d been developing since his Fifth Symphony, brought to its highest level of sophistication.

EK: And what about Mahler’s finale? Does it follow a similar pattern to Tchaikovsky’s?

DB: Indeed it does. Like Tchaikovsky, Mahler’s finale shifts from looking back to a passionate, reflective view of the present. But for Mahler, it’s about acceptance – of himself, his past, and his journey. It’s not a farewell to life but a profound self-realization and the ultimate expression of his slow-movement style.

EK: Both composers were summing up their life’s work in these symphonies.

Capstones to Their Artistic Journeys

DB: Exactly. Tchaikovsky and Mahler used their final symphonies not as mournful farewells but as capstones to their artistic journeys. Each movement in both works represents the composers at their finest, showcasing the elements of their style that they had honed throughout their careers.

An audience immersed in an Inside Out Concert by David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City. Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

This approach transforms how we understand these works. Rather than viewing them through the lens of impending death, we can appreciate them as the ultimate achievements of composers at the height of their powers, pushing boundaries and achieving new levels of expression.

EK: How did you come to see these works in this way?

DB: While studying the first movement of Tchaikovsky’s Pathétique, I discovered that Tchaikovsky directly quoted the “heartbeat” rhythm from Strauss’ tone poem “Death and Transfiguration” in the horns. I had already perceived the relationship between the First Movement and Romeo and Juliet. Hence, the combination strongly suggests Tchaikovsky was returning to his younger self and reimagining Romeo and Juliet. The relationship between the 2nd movement, his Ballet Waltzes, the 3rd movement, and his symphonic finales was clarified. It was clear that Tchaikovsky was showcasing his best artistic voice, finally free from the shackles of convention. This view contributes to how his newly imagined “Romeo and Juliet” was written in blindingly brilliant three days, unlike the original ten years.

The “Sigh” Motif

EK: What led you to your view of Mahler’s Ninth?

DB: Mahler doesn’t waste time giving us his heartbeat rhythm at the start of the First Movement, but he continues with a “sigh” motif embedded throughout the First Movement that directly quotes the “sigh” motif from the introduction of “Death and Transfiguration,” occurring from the 4th quarter note to the 1st quarter note of the next measure. With the “lookback” narrative activated, we can see the relationship between his First Movement and the youthful music of the First Symphony, how the Second Movement perfects his use of dance forms, particularly Ländlers, and waltzes, and how the third movement showcases what I call his “Grand Style” of counterpoint.

Richard Strauss (1904). This photograph of Richard Strauss was taken in New York during his US tour that year. Public Domain

As I dug further, I learned that Mahler and Strauss were good friends, and Mahler was quite obsessed with “Death and Transfiguration.” He repeatedly asked Strauss for a copy of the score. What’s even more telling is that when Mahler became Music Director of the New York Philharmonic in the years following the completion of his Ninth Symphony, he programmed “Death and Transfiguration” three times in a single season. This shows how deeply the work resonated with him and how its narrative inspired the Ninth Symphony.

Death and Transfiguration

EK: That’s insightful and fascinating. How did this discovery change your understanding of these symphonies?

DB: It completely transformed my perspective for each. I began to see how Tchaikovsky and Mahler used their final symphonies as artistic reflection and summation, much like the old man in “Death and Transfiguration” looking back on his life. This approach of reimagining and perfecting core elements of their style across each movement mirrors the reflective journey in “Death and Transfiguration.” It suggests that both composers were at the height of their powers, using their mastery to create works that encapsulated and elevated the themes and techniques they had developed throughout their careers.

EK: Your insights into these works is profound. How do you hope this perspective will impact and inform the audience’s experience of the Festival?

A Revelatory Experience

DB: My deepest hope is that attendees will leave with a newfound appreciation for Mahler’s genius and a desire to explore his other works. Whether you’re a seasoned Mahler enthusiast or a curious newcomer, the “Beginnings and Endings” festival promises to be a revelatory experience.

EK: Please describe more about the specific performances and the orchestras involved in the Festival.

DB: Certainly. We’re thrilled to have the Massapequa Philharmonic performing Mahler’s First Symphony on October 27th at 3 PM at Berner Auditorium in Massapequa. Then, on November 24th at 5 PM, the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony will tackle the formidable Ninth Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music.

David Bernard on stage with the Massapequa Philharmonic. Courtesy of the Massapequa Philharmonic

We’re not just presenting concerts; we’re offering a journey through the heart and mind of one of music’s most visionary creators. Through our performances and pre-concert discussions, we aim to equip listeners with the tools to deeply appreciate these complex works and perhaps ignite a lifelong passion for Mahler’s music. In addition, the performance of Mahler’s Ninth will be presented as an InsideOut Concerts Event, where the audience experiences the work immersively from within the orchestra—a powerful and once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

EK: Finally, what would you say to someone who’s never experienced Mahler’s music? Why should they attend this Festival?

DB: Mahler once said, “A symphony must be like the world. It must contain everything.” His music is a journey through the full spectrum of human emotion and experience. For newcomers, this Festival offers a perfect introduction. The First Symphony showcases Mahler’s innovative use of folk melodies, sounds of nature, and orchestral colors. With its poignant beauty, the Ninth demonstrates how he pushed the boundaries of symphonic form to express profound philosophical ideas.

Explore the Depths of Human Experience

By attending both concerts, audience members will witness firsthand the incredible evolution of one of history’s greatest composers. It’s a chance to be moved, challenged, and ultimately transformed by the power of Mahler’s music. We’re not just offering concerts; we’re providing an opportunity to explore the depths of human experience through sound.

EK: Thank you for these profound insights. It sounds like an extraordinary event for music lovers of all backgrounds.

DB: Thank you. We’re excited to share this musical adventure with our audience and hope to see many new faces at the Festival. It’s a unique opportunity to experience Mahler’s world in a way that’s both accessible and deeply rewarding.

David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony standing for bows to thunderous applause. Courtesy Massapequa Philharmonic

The “Beginnings and Endings” Mahler Festival, featuring the Massapequa Philharmonic and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony, takes place on October 27th and November 24th.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

I don’t often talk about the actors first.

Let me just start off by saying that both actors are divine. The play The Ask, by Matthew Freeman, gives them both a plethora of opportunities to express the depth of their characters and transcend a presentation and become real people, locked in real human conflict, and involved in a beautiful dance of finding common ground and understanding.

The play is very good (see below) but the acting is phenomenal. Betsy Aidem (as Greta, a wealthy donor to causes close to her heart) brings a life lived to the stage (she nailed the phone conversation and made it a performance unto itself). What she presented in her acting was a past, present, and future that gave reason and cause to her character’s utterances and actions. Colleen Litchfield (as Tanner, a young neophyte at fund raising) presented a striving vulnerability that kept the continuous feeling of on-shaky-ground and out-of-their-depth ever present. So much so that I’m sure I’m not the only audience member that wanted to give reassurance when they became overwhelmed and broke down. Both actors did such a good job that you’re able to forget that they’re working and watch them living the play.

This is a world premier. The Ask is based on Matthew Freeman’s thirteen years of fundraising experience for the ACLU. His dialogue is crisp, nimble, and captivating. The issues raised are now. The play is a ride with your social morals casually flapping in the breeze looking for a flagstaff to affix themselves to. When you’re able to give great actors wonderful things to say, purpose in saying them, and meat for the mind to chew on, you’ve got a play worth watching.

Tanner, newly hired and assigned to find out why past large donor’s have not donated, arrives at Greta’s New York apartment to persuade her to 5x her past donation. Called upon to defend the national organization and the many mis-steps it has incurred (who could?) Tanner is in un-chartered territory. All Greta is really looking for is acknowledgment of her grievances and a human connection, but this age of being hyper politically correct, inhibits this connection.

I also want to make note of Craig Napoliello’s highly detailed realistic set. It’s a NY apartment we’ve all seen and are familiarly comfortable with filled with a life of living. It adds immensely to the performances, grounding them in a place and time.

A very good play with great actors.

—–

A world premiere of Matthew Freeman’s The Ask, directed by Jessi D. Hill, and presented at the wild project (195 E 3rd St, New York, NY 10009), September 6-28.

The performance runs approximately 80 minutes, with no intermission. Tickets can be bought HERE.

The production stars Betsy Aidem as Greta and Colleen Litchfield as Tanner.
The creative team includes Scenic Design by Craig Napoliello, Lighting Design by Daisy Long, Sound Design by Cody Hom, and Costume Design by Nicole Wee.

title.rendered: Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

New York – Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park

It was a beautiful summer night at Bryant Park in New York City as thousands assembled to see and hear the fabulous American Symphony Orchestra. From the onset, one was struck with the charm and nostalgia of live music in the village square, with visitors, families, and friends sitting on benches, blankets, or chairs, enjoying the same experience. People sitting on blankets or in chairs chatting occasionally, the hum of their voices blending with the music, but far softer and less urgent than in the busy streets.

Towering skyscrapers and Leon Botstein conducting Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Communal Entertainment

The setting holds a deep sense of history, evoking memories of summer nights, outdoor festivals, or small-town celebrations, where music was a form of communal entertainment before the rise of digital entertainment. It evokes reminders of simpler times when live performances were a prime source of joy and connection.

Despite being in the city and surrounded by broad avenues and skyscrapers, Bryant Park has trees and grassy areas where one might hear leaves rustling in the breeze or the faint chirping of birds or crickets in quiet moments. Of note was the striking contrast between the subtle qualities of the music and the ever-present city noises in the background. But as listeners were drawn into the music, they escaped from the city’s sirens, engines, horns, and footsteps as the cacophony of bustling sounds grew more distant.

In essence, tonight’s concert by the American Symphony Orchestra was more than a concert of superb music; it was a celebration of communal heritage interwoven with the fabric of small-town life. It was an experience with a timeless quality, where modern life meets a gentler, more connected past.

Leon Botstein describes the music Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Insightful, Inspirational Exordiums

Maestro Leon Botstein opened the concert with introductions and the first of his insightful, inspirational exordiums about each musical work to be performed. Considering tonight’s collection of luminescent, brilliant works, Botstein explained that music can tell stories and support and project theatrical experiences. That’s clearly seen in the film genre. Many of my comments about the works performed are derived from Botstein’s exceptional descriptions. The ASO began with Scott Joplin’s Treemonisha, a rare blend of classical operatic structure with ragtime rhythms for which Joplin was most famous. Botstein noted the resurgence of Joplin’s music after its predominant role in David S. Ward’s film The Sting. Released in 1973, The Sting was directed by George Roy Hill and starred Paul Newman and Robert Redford.

Winning several Academy Awards, The Sting is notable for its clever plot centered around two con men in 1930s Chicago and its use of Scott Joplin’s ragtime music, particularly “The Entertainer.” It also incorporates African American folk songs, spirituals, and traditional call-and-response forms. This fusion was groundbreaking at the time, as it combined the high-art form of opera with the rhythms and styles of African American popular music, making it accessible and artistically complex.

Cellos and Basses on stage in Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Identity and Cultural Pride

Next, the ASO performed Florence Price’s Suite of Dances, a vibrant, culturally rich composition combining African American musical traditions with classical forms. It featured fusions of rhythmic energy, melodic beauty, orchestral color, and a celebration of dance. As a product of an African American woman composing in the early 20th century, Price’s Suite of Dances resonates with themes of identity and cultural pride. The suite honors the African American experience, incorporating dance and music traditions familiar to Black communities at the time while making these traditions accessible to the concert hall.

Psycho

Bernard Hermann’s Psycho Suite is based on his score for Alfred Hitchcock’s groundbreaking film Psycho. Herrmann employed leitmotif, notably a three-note descending motif associated with Norman Bates’s troubled psyche. This minimalist approach mirrored the simplicity and emotional depth of the film’s themes, underscoring the duality in Norman’s character and the psychological complexity of the narrative.

For tonight’s listeners recalling the visual and dramatic elements of Hitchcock’s oeuvre, many indeed experienced quivering horripilation from the spare, haunting qualities of Herrmann’s score.

Maestro Leon Botstein conducting in Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

The orchestra ably projected Herrmann’s modernist score, which relies on dissonance to display cinematic unease in the film’s gripping, mysterious, tragic circumstances. While unresolved chordal tensions, delicious discordance, and edgy harmonies amplified the film’s atmosphere of dread, these elements ably reflected the characters’ chaotic mental states. They added to an overall sense of volatility and uncertainty. Hitchcock famously said, “33% of the effect of Psycho was due to the music.”

The power of this music set against the backdrop of city sounds was almost psychedelic in its sonic clarity.

High and Low Culture

Kurt Weill’s Dreiggroschenmusik (Three Penny Opera) followed with its jaunty, catchy tunes, including the song Mack the Knife, famously recorded by Bobby Darin. This work bridges the gap between high and low culture (culture haute et basse) by merging classical forms with popular music, jazz, and cabaret elements. Drawing on the bon vivant style of 1920s Berlin, Weill blends operatic structures with the sounds of street music and dance halls. This mixture was modern and radical, challenging the separation between “serious” music and everyday entertainment.

Members of the orchestra in Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

The change in instrumentation we witnessed was delightful. As most of the orchestra left the stage, an unusual ensemble that included banjo, saxophone, piano, and percussion alongside some traditional orchestral instruments arrived. This idiosyncratic ensemble helped create the work’s distinctive sound, blending the brashness of street music with refined orchestration. The banjo and saxophone contributed to the suite’s jazz and cabaret influences, giving it a raw, urban quality.

Three Penny Opera

Readers may recall the 1954 revival of Weill’s Three Penny Opera at the Theatre de Lys (later renamed the Lucille Lortel Theatre) in Greenwich Village. Directed by Carmen Capalbo and produced by Stanley Chase, this production was performed in English, with a translation by Marc Blitzstein preserving the satirical edge of Bertolt Brecht’s text while bolstering accessibility to American audiences. The revival ran for an astonishing 2,707 performances over seven years, making it one of the longest-running Off-Broadway shows in history at the time.

A view of the Empire State Building spire at Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Leonard Bernstein

The concert finished with Leonard Bernstein’s Three Dance Episodes from “On the Town.” This was a perfect choice to close a splendid concert in New York City. Though only three movements, the Three Dance Episodes cover a broad emotional spectrum, from the exuberance and brash confidence of “The Great Lover” to the quiet introspection of “Lonely Town” to the explosive, celebratory energy of “Times Square, 1944.” This expressive resourcefulness is a hallmark of Bernstein’s work, demonstrating his ability to capture complex human emotions in a way that resonates with audiences.

Psycho 1960 film (Madame Tussauds) by Max Langenbeck from Germany, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons

The American Symphony Orchestra is a superb organization led by the acclaimed conductor, music director, and educator Leon Botstein. Check their website for an exciting season of splendid music.

Beyond The Hall by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park

Leon Botstein, Conductor

American Symphony Orchestra

1330 Avenue of the Americas
Suite 23A
New York, NY 10019
212-868-9276 info@americansymphony.org
For tickets and information, go to https://americansymphony.org/current-season/

Readers may also enjoy our reviews of Opera in the Garden by OnSite Opera, Norm Lewis at 54 Below, Tony Danza, Meg Okura at the Met Museum, Laura Benanti at the Minetta Lane Theater, Brazilian Jazz at Le Bab Ilo in Paris, and Marilyn Maye birthday celebration at 54 Below.

content.rendered:
By Vicki Weisfeld

Congratulate The Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey for producing a version of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility that lives up to its title! It showcases both a fine theatrical sense and the complicated interpersonal sensibilities of the classic story. Adapted by British playwright, theatre director, and screenwriter Jessica Swale and directed for STNJ by Nisi Sturgis, it opened September 7 and closes September 22.

You know the story. It’s in 1797 England that we find the Dashwood family, comprising a widow (played by Lynette R. Freeman) and her three daughters—Elinor (Mandi Masden), a model of good sense, Marianne of heightened feelings (Billie Wyatt), and inquisitive, adolescent Margaret (Terra Chaney). A conniving sister-in-law (Kayla Ryan Walsh) deprives them of their inheritance, and they must retire to a modest country life. The two older girls are of marriageable age, and Elinor falls for Edward Ferrars (Patrick Andrew Jones), previously engaged in secret and seemingly unattainable; Marianne falls for the dashing Willoughby (Christian Frost) who returns her affection, and she is also adored by mature, reliable—and therefore unappealing—Colonel Brandon (Sean Mahan).

That group of actors makes up most of the cast, except for utility infielder Patrick Toon, who appears in many guises and has dozens of offstage costume changes, portraying every character distinctly and perfectly. In fact, except for the two older sisters (Masden and Wyatt), all cast members play multiple roles, including that of stagehand. It was a particular pleasure to see Chaney move so convincingly from little sister and budding naturalist to sly fiancée to a street gossip. These multiple personas all work, except when Mrs. Dashwood reappears as Willoughby’s fiancée. The age difference was insurmountable, but all the other female cast members were otherwise engaged, one might say. Masden and Wyatt’s strong performances make you yearn for the happiness of these young women.

Swale’s adaptation is faithful to the novel and some of the judicious cuts Emma Thompson made for the 1995 screenplay. Fidelity to material and memory produces deep associations, even if act one does become rather long. The versatile set nicely accommodates, with some well-choreographed rearrangements of furniture, the various houses, rooms, and outdoor settings where the story takes place, leaving much to the imagination except for lovely verdure.

Austen’s works, including this one, continue to capture audiences by their fundamental emotional truths. The characters in Sense and Sensibility are trapped in the conventions of their time—women didn’t work or inherit, honorable men lived up to their marital commitments—yet most find their way to happiness in ways that satisfy them and the audiences of today. Modern constraints may be different, but they nevertheless exist.

Production credits to Brittany Vasta (set design), Anthony Galaska (lighting design), Liam Bellman-Sharpe (sound design; original music), Kimiye Corwin (dance consultant), Sophie S. Schneider (lovely costumes), and Julie Foh (dialect consultant).

STNJ productions are hosted at Drew University in Madison, N.J. (easily reachable from NYC by train). For tickets, call the box office at 973-408-5600 or visit the Box Office online.

excerpt.rendered: Jane Austen’s characters strain against the conventions of two centuries ago, yet their yearning for love is timeless. Audiences are loving this beautiful and beautifully acted production at the Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey.

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

It is not every Off-Broadway musical that boasts a chorus of 12 real-life healthcare professionals. Then again, it is unlikely there has ever been a musical quite as concerned with antibiotic-resistant bacteria as Lifeline. Germinated at the 2018 Edinburgh Fringe Festival under the title, The Mould That Changed The World, this revised staging, triple in length from the original, is not only a chronicle of the discovery of penicillin, but a loud warning as to the medical dangers we face in a world corrupted by the misuse and overuse of antibiotics. There’s also dancing and love songs.

Penned by Becky Hope-Palmer and Robin Hiley, and featuring an all-UK principal cast in addition to the dozen locals from area medical centers, the production gets its main point across effectively, if repetitiously, attacking the issue with three interwoven plotlines. If at times the action becomes disjointed or meandering, the solid performances and sheer novelty and importance of the subject matter are an effective antidote. Rather than preaching to the audience, Hope-Palmer supplies vivid examples of just how damaging antimicrobial resistance can be, leaving us justifiably cautious as we return home to our overstuffed medicine cabinets.

Scottish physician Alexander Flemming is credited with discovering penicillin and it is he, as embodied in a strong-willed and powerfully sung performance by Matthew Malthouse, who opens the show with the work’s thesis, “There is the danger that the ignorant man may easily underdose himself, and by exposing his microbes to non-lethal quantities of the drug, make them resistant.” Throughout the first act we follow Flemming’s journey in reverse chronology, from 1952 when he touts the dangers of using his discovery in too small a quantity, back to 1928 when his moldy petri dish reveals a miracle cure. Along the way, his colleague, Amalia (Nicole Raquel Dennis), waltzes into his arms, becoming his second wife (though, mysteriously, not a mention to be had of spouse number one or their son).

Intercut with Flemming’s story is a present-day tale of three friends. Jess (Kirsty MacLaren) is a junior doctor at the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary. Julian (Robbie Scott) is a political staffer on the rise, and Jess’ would-be romantic partner Aaron (Scott McClure) is a musician who finds himself under her care, recovering from colon cancer but with a post-op infection that leads to dire consequences.

And, rattling both storylines, the chorus, portraying present-day docs, recites a litany of case studies, exemplifying brutal contemporary agonies observed by medical pros on a first name basis with their patients, “We’ve just confirmed the infection has destroyed Gina’s aortic valve.”

Act Two tends to wander, beginning with a speech from Jess that recounts what is already known, and dwelling on Aaron’s mother, Layla (the charismatic Mari McGinlay), as she copes with her son’s tragedy. But when it gets down to business, there are scenes that make a bold statement on how governments historically fail to act in the people’s best interest. Flashing back to World War One, an upstart Dr. Flemming cannot convince the War Office to end its use of dangerous antiseptics to treat wounded soldiers, while in present day London, Julian is equally powerless in getting funding from the NHS for Jess’ cause.

Hiley’s score is most effective when it shines light on how our comfort with modern medicine has led to the problem at hand, “Although infection can’t be traced/Here is some Fluclox just in case.” Alice McNicholas’ costumes are on point and instrumental in keeping the timelines straight, but the rest of the creative team’s efforts are not doing the cast any favors. Too often, scenes are dimly lit or performed behind a scrim or upon a dizzying turntable or behind a half-wall or too far upstage or interrupted with needless video segments. In a show that begs intimacy, the overall mood is one of distance, at least until the play’s final moments when the chorus members come into the audience to introduce their true selves, offering rays of hope in doing so.

 

Lifeline – By Becky Hope-Palmer, Music and Lyrics by Robin Hiley; Directed by Alex Howarth.

WITH: Matthew Malthouse (Alexander Fleming), Kirsty MacLaren (Jess), Scott McClure (Aaron / Clowes), Robbie Scott (Julian / Pryce), Nicole Raquel Dennis (Amalia / Ensemble), Mari McGinlay (Layla / Ensemble), Richard Lounds (Ensemble), Sarah Haddath (Ensemble) and Graham Richardson (Ensemble).

Neil Metcalfe, musical director; Wayne Parsons, choreography; Alice McNicholas, set and costume design; Will Monks, Lighting design; Paul Smith, sound design. Charades Theatre Company at The Pershing Square Signature Center, 480 W. 42nd St.,  212-739-7875, https://www.lifelinemusical.com/. Through September 28. Running time: 2 hours 25 minutes

By Victoria Dammer

Isaac Mizrahi in person is a once-in-a-lifetime gift not to be missed.  There’s talent. Then there’s something else that only decades as an actor, TV host, writer, designer, producer, and singer can bring you. That one-of-a-kind phenomenon I’ve described, Isaac Mizrahi, currently appears at 54 Below for a limited engagement, and if there is one seat available, grab it fast.

Mizrahi had an uncanny ability to engage the sold-out crowd as he told personal stories, sang several tunes with his band, and brought the multiple-aged crowd almost to tears of laughter with his intellectually stimulating humor.

Leslie Berkman, from New York, commented, “He’s fantastic. From beginning to end, non-stop entertainment.” She follows him on Instagram and first saw him in person in Mamaroneck. Berkman was treating her soon-to-be-married daughter to a special night out, and that’s a testament to how appealing Mizrahi is to younger and older audiences.

Mizrahi bounded onto the stage in a black tux-style suit and white shirt with a bow over a foot wide, and the audience greeted him with loud applause. He’s a man with a sexy, animated voice who’s often in the spotlight. Yet he was gracious to acknowledge his band right away. Mizrahi said, “I got a note I objectified my band.” He also toasted the audience for coming out on a sultry night in New York City. The show got hotter from here.

Mizrahi opened with the song Come Live with Me, from Valley of the Dolls, written by Dory and André Previn. It’s a song with an invitation to be with someone, if only for a day, and Mizrahi’s use of its message was heartwarming.

His second tune, Cole Porter’s The Laziest Girl in Town, was what Mizrahi called his autobiographical song. It featured a heavy trumpet solo by James Sarna. Part of the song reads: “Nothing ever worries me, No one hurries me, I take pleasure leisurely, Even when I kiss.” Admittedly, Mizrahi gave the audience insight into his identity with those four lines. That is stunning.

Mizrahi’s surprise guest star was actor, producer, and singer Alyssa Milano. The two met while working on Project Runway. Mizrahi jokingly commented on her wardrobe, “That is literally the ugliest dress I’ve ever seen.” Milano will make her Broadway debut as Roxie Hart in the musical Chicago on September 16th. She and Mizrahi sang the Chicago hit “Nowadays.”

Mizrahi claimed he was guilty of cultural whiplash, performing an additional Cole Porter song, You’re the Top, then moving on to Billie Eilish’s hit from the movie Barbie, What Was I Made For? The audience didn’t care as Ben Waltzer treated them to a resounding piano solo in What Was I Made For?

The encore was a powerful version of You and Me, and anyone in the audience could be sure that when experiencing Mizrahi’s fantastic performance, this is how he looks at all his supporters.

Isaac Mizrahi: A Brief History, at 54 Below, with guest star Alyssa Milano. Music Director/Piano by Ben Waltzer, Drums by Daniel Duke, Bass by Joe Strasser, and Trumpet by James Sarno. Press by Matt Gross, Heart Spade PR. Instagram and TikTok: @imisaacmizrahi

THROUGH AUGUST 31 at 54 Below.  Tickets HERE

content.rendered:
By David Walters
“Something must break when the hurricane blows.”
—

Hurricane Season by Sawyer Estes, produced by Atlanta-based Vernal & Sere Theatre, is an undefinable piece of innovative art that resists being put in a box with a well-marked label. Originally presented in 2022, it is currently making its, and the company’s, New York debut at Theatre Row.

There is a duality, a triality, and a quadrality that is constant for the two-hour production as script, set, and sound clash and meld together to present the character’s longing of life, desperately seeking to come through it with purpose and meaning. Beyond the omnipresent noise of the world, silence and strong physical movement also have their say in the production giving each character time to sense where they are and what they are trying to achieve and voicing a deep angst in the physicality.

Death doulas often say there are basically four things people lament at the very end: I wish I could tell them I love them; I wish they would say they love me; I wish I could apologize; I wish they would apologize to me. All of that is part of each character’s journey. All of that is encapsulated in Hurricane Season.

Looking back I realize that all I’ve said about the production so far is a bit ethereal and not very revealing. Certainly not enough clarity for you to decide if it’s wise to spend your money and your time.

The basic throughline is a non-communicative, middle-class, middle-aged couple no longer being fulfilled within, go without and travel around the globe to seek out completeness in younger sexual partners that resemble them. They bring their soul/hole fillers back home to a house that has been struck by a hurricane and the 100+ year old tree right outside has come crashing down (symbolism).  But this is only one of the layers, as the multi-facited set and omni-present soundscape add further layers and commentary about living in a comfortable middle-class existence while wars, rumors of wars, and climate destruction ravage about them. Despite the deep roots of societal normality that the couple built together, they long for something else and seek to find it, perhaps losing themselves even further.

This is a play for both your mind and your senses; something you won’t easily forget.

—

Hurricane Season was written and directed by Sawyer Estes.

The Company: Erin Boswell, Pascal Portney, Melissa Rainey, Sam Ross, and Kathrine Barnes.

The creative team: Erin O’Connor (movement direction and assistant director), Josh Oberlander (scenic design), Lindsey Sharpless (lighting design and stage manager), Matthew Shively, (projection design), Zach Halaby and Kacie Willis (sound design), Mitch Butler (sound engineer), and Monty Wilson (production manager and scenic construction).

It runs August 23 – September 7, 2024, at Theatre Row in Theatre Four, located at 410 W 42nd St in Manhattan. The running time is 2 hours plus one intermission. Tickets, which start at $45, are available at www.hurricaneseasonplay.com.

title.rendered: I Love You Because at Green Room 42

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

“I Love You Because” is a love letter to love and New York. It was uplifting, but not particularly innovative.

This was an hour-long reading of the musical at the Green Room 42–with a queer twist. It focused on two couples over the course of their coming-to-be couples, with two bartender-narrators helpfully at their sides.

It’s a New York play through and through. They sing about how beautiful New York is when you’re in love. And…immediately there’s a cheating boyfriend.

Austin Bennet (Mark Bacon) discovers his boyfriend is cheating on him. So, Austin heads onto dating apps with no intention of finding love. Indeed, he spends the first date with Marty Fitzwilliams (Cal Mitchell) talking about his exes. All of them.

Normally, Marty might have jumped ship. But he’s not here for love, he’s here for a rebound. Diana Bingley (Ally Bonino) just walked him through the math behind rebound time through her song “Actuary Time.” In the song, an absolute stand out from the show, she goes through all of the variables, the multiples, the facts, and the theory to come up with a number: six months. Because of the math she explains to him, he needs to find Mr. Wrong so he can, after six months, find Mr. Right. So, he’s here on this date to find Mr. Wrong. And off the bat, we have a situation with the couple who’s there more so for the ride than for each other.

Sometime after Marty and Austin go on their first date, they meet in a coffee shop. All of a sudden, Marty is confronting Austin. It’s not a bad confrontation–namely, there’s truth to it. However, because of the pacing, it just feels like it’s coming out of nowhere. Throughout the show, that pacing throws in a few unfortunate wrinkles that make it really hard for me to actually root for or believe in the relationships in the musical.

Time goes on. Side characters intervene. The narrators sing: “people tell us YOU’LL FIND the one if you just look, we guarantee it. Well I’ve LOOKED AND LOOKED and there’s no one for me.” Marty and Austin recall the sense of frustration with love and dating in New York and also realize that they have found something special in each other and get back together. And we have a happy ending.

The music was fun and upbeat and the show is sweet. But the script definitely has room for improvement. My biggest qualm was the pacing: it was FAST. There’s very little sense of time passing. Because of that, many decisions don’t make sense-  which makes me wish we had had a full adaptation, or any adaptation longer than an hour.

I Love You Because by Ryan Cunningham and Joshua Salzman, directed by Colin Hanlon

WITH Mark Bacon as “Austin Bennet,” Cal Mitchell as “Marty Fitzwilliams,” Deven Kolluri as “Jeff Bennet,” Ally Bonino as “Diana Bingley,” Nicole Zelka as “NYC Person 1,” and Coleman Cummings as “NYC Person 2.”

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Chain Theatre’s summer 2024 One-Act Festival is bigger (over 50 plays), badder (many debuts), and more extensive than ever. With fourteen programs (evenings) to choose from of two to five one-acts, you can’t go wrong as something in there will catch your fancy. In fact, ask a friend for a number from one to fourteen without telling them what it’s for, and go to that evening. You won’t be disappointed.

PROGRAM #14 

CATCH by Jeryl Brunner

I’m sensing that this is a somewhat autobiographical exploration of the taut trials and travails of dating life for the author moved to a higher realm via comedy and adroitly directed by Sara Thigpen.

Justine (playwright Jeryl Brunner), although mainly choosing to be alone in her 40s, still yearns for a relationship. She did go out on, what she considered, a successful date with Craig (Jason Kravits) but he has never called her back despite promising to do so. They keep awkwardly running into each other on the street triggering Justine’s innate sense of self doubt. There is a well acted flashback as kids that sheds light on her inhibiting demeanor. Craig is an avid fly fisherman and Justine happens to know a bit about the sport and the lingo from her job as a fact checker. Nevertheless, she consistently feels like a pinball “bumped around, thrown in every direction” instead of the flipper flinging the ball every which way. She learns by the end of the play to cut bait and become her own flipper.

BANSHEE by John Patrick Shanley

This is a delightful New York premier of Shanley’s one-act play that dives into fantasy, swims several laps around the stage doing the back stroke, and triumphantly emerges from the deep end. An Irish banshee named Genevieve (the charmingly spirited pixieish Elizabeth Bays)  pops up in the apartment of Malcolm (Eric Betancourt), sick (to death?) with the flu and tries to convince him to have a half-banshee/half-human baby in order to quell the sadness that surrounds her (banshees are the harbingers of death). Not knowing how babies are made she’s a bit repulsed by the crudeness of the baby making act. A kiss from Genevieve immediately eradicates Malcom’s flu and he is smitten. The play touches on what it’s like to go against our very natures and the consternation of who we believe we are.

HANGMEN by Kyle C. Mumford

Years of therapy haven’t helped and Bruce (Mark Gorham), a middle aged man, is at the end of his rope. He climbs a tree with the intent to end it all and hang himself. Just as he’s about to take the final leap he notices he’s being stared at from the tree next door and it pulls him up short. It’s Omar (David Harrison Pralgo) a twenty-something also at the end of his rope preparing to step off his branch into the unknown. They each challenge the other to go first and flip back and forth sharing the feelings that brought them to their respective branches realizing that they are not as alone as they had originally thought. A surprise from another tree eventually gets them both down to commiserate about the cards that life has dealt them culminating with the poignant thought that even in the darkest forests, light sometimes can find its way through.

SOURED MILK by Annie Raczko

Is another play that seems to stem from real life. It’s the teacher’s break room at a high school with a newly appointed young untested principal (Josh Bartosch) who shies away from the difficulties of his position with forced humor that never lands well. Also in attendance are Barbara (Annie Raczko) the union rep who doesn’t want her name attached to anything for fear of reprisal, the always up but means well Cindy (Olivia Whicheloe) who proselytizes healthy living with yoga and crystals, and Sam (Crystal Williamson) who has been here forever and never wants to leave as her position at the school has become the only thing that defines her. It’s outlandish parents (please use your right hand when writing on the board as it upsets the right handed students), budget cuts that require someone losing their job, absenteeism that has become rampant, and the spoiled milk in the fridge that no one will take responsibility for. Each of the characters are distinct in their wants, needs, and hopes and dreams for themselves personally, and why they do what they do as teachers. It’s a compelling look into a difficult world that we are all glad that someone feels chosen to do, but mostly glad it’s not us. Teachers deserve more of everything.

———-

Chain Theatre / 3rd floor

312 West 36th Street New York City, NY 10018

Tickets and schedule through September 1: HERE

content.rendered:
By Victoria L. Dammer

The creative arts have cultivated some of the greatest and most sensual love affairs throughout history. Actor Elizabeth Taylor discussed her passion for Richard Burton, saying, “When I saw him on the set of Cleopatra, we were always madly and powerfully in love.” Painter Pablo Picasso had several wives and mistresses who influenced his artwork. King Edward VIII gave up his crown for a woman, saying, “I have found it impossible to carry the heavy burden…without the help and support of the woman I love.”

Anton Chekhov and Olga Knipper

Dear Anton! Dear Olga! a play written and directed by Tatiana Korinfsky, masterfully captures one of the most passionate relationships in theater history. A series of telegrams and letters of love and longing between Russia’s famous playwright Anton Chekhov (Eric Kuzmuk) and stage actress Olga Knipper (Snezhana Chernova), are read out loud. The audience realizes the pain both felt because of separation; Knipper spent most of her time in Moscow and Chekhov spent his in Yalta in the late 1800s.

Chekhov, Ibsen and Strindberg

Chekhov was born impoverished in Southern Russia and was heavily influenced by his mother, an exceptional storyteller. To financially provide for his family during his schooling, he wrote short and humorous stories. Alongside Henrik Ibsen and August Strindberg, he influenced the Modernist writing style.

The Seagull

Chekhov wrote the novella-length short story The Steppe, a play entitled Ivanov, a critical success and The Seagull, and others. Knipper, an original member of the Moscow Art Theatre, met Russia’s most eligible literary bachelor while rehearsing The Seagull in Moscow. Thus, their correspondence and love affair began and lasted until his death.

Tuberculosis and mood-swings

Chekhov’s letter and telegrams to Olga reflected the miserable gloom of Russia. He complained of his poor health, afflicted with tuberculosis. Knipper’s writing to the playwright exhibited her well-known temper and mood swings.

Theatergoer Ibragim Soliev, from Chikola, Vladikavkaz, said “The overall subdued temperament of Chekhov and Knipper’s communications comes from a society where love and passion are rarely displayed in writing. It’s important to understand the temperament of society at the time the letters were written.” Patron Nicki Cochrane said she “waited 50 years to see such exquisite work.”

Knipper summarizes the angst Chekhov and Knipper had about their footprint in history. “Will we be remembered in 50 years? Will we touch any lives?” Dear Anton! Dear Olga! is the performance that confirms their legacy. Just as important, Chernova and Kuzmuk’s performances were remarkable and unforgettable, and the standing ovation supported the sentiment.

 

Dear Anton! Dear Olga!, at the Polaris North Studio for a limited engagement. Written and directed by Tatiana Korinfsky. Starring Snezhana Chernova and Eric Kuzmuk, with Jeannie Dalton and Andrew Rothkin. Set/costume design by Tatiana Korinfsky and Lighting/sound by Keithlyn B. Parkman.

title.rendered: Kenny Barron Trio at Smoke Jazz – Through August 25

content.rendered:
NEW YORK – Kenny Barron Trio at Smoke Jazz Club

Acclaimed pianist Kenny Barron showed how to break it down with his trio at Smoke Jazz Club in New York City. With Kenny Barron on piano, Peter Washington on bass, and Savannah Harris on drums, these cats displayed sublime musical artistry. It was an extraordinary, history-making night of glorious, tingling, and overwhelming music. The trio is in residence through August 25, so you must move quickly to get seats.

L-R: Pianist Kenny Barron, Bassist Peter Washington, and Drummer Savannah Harris. Photos by Edward Kliszus

Smoke’s intimate atmosphere was enhanced by subtle lighting, a great menu, superb sound, and a Steinway grand piano tuned to studio perfection. Tonight was the perfect venue for projecting Barron’s poetic, crystalline purity of creative genius.

After the host introduced the Kenny Barron trio, the bespoke and cool Barron chuckled about a charming reference to his status as “the late” artist (the host didn’t actually say this).

L-R: Portraits of George and Ira Gershwin. Photo of G. Gershwin by Carl Van Vechten. Photos Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

The concert opened with George and Ira Gershwin’s “Embraceable You,” a perfect choice that showcased Barron’s ability to balance romanticism with a modern harmonic sensibility. The lush chords and melodic lines emerged from a delicate yet assured touch.

Kenny Barron Trio poster outside the Smoke Jazz Club in New York City. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Barron’s opening was sublime and gorgeous, setting a tender tone with delicate shadings and sonority before being joined by Washington and Harris. His attention to and use of subtle harmonic shifts, dissonance, melodic/harmonic tensions, and chromatic interplay was exquisite. With this song and the others tonight, ample time was provided for the trio’s improvisational interplay and unity. While each song opened with the head and followed the changes while improvising, transitions were seamless, and solos were virtuosic and sensitively synced with fellow artists. The trio exemplified deep musical and creative connections.

Duke Ellington (1964). Photo: Public domain

Barron’s followed with solo performances of Duke Ellington‘s works. This graceful, glittering set of songs was a masterclass in reflective, expressive, and improvisatory piano playing. Pieces like “Lotus Blossom,” “A Flower is a Lonesome Thing,” “Melancholia,” and “Star-Crossed Lovers” highlighted Barron’s ability to convey deep emotion through his instrument, capturing the halcyon elegance and quintessence of Ellington’s compositions with radiance and gentle splendor. Barron’s interpretation was reflective and meditative, with the music breathing and connecting with the listeners. Barron’s use of space and dynamics was especially striking, creating lyric ecstasy and moments of profound stillness.

The trio ventured into Thelonious Monk‘s repertoire, offering an up-tempo rendition of “Well You Needn’t” and a ballad version of “Ask Me Now.” Barron’s interpretation of Monk was respectful and inventive, preserving the angularity and wit of Monk’s compositions through his unique voice.

Thelonious Monk, Minton’s Playhouse, New York, N.Y., ca. Sept. 1947 (William P. Gottlieb 06191) Public Domain

Barron’s ability to navigate Monk’s idiosyncratic rhythms and harmonies with precision and creativity was a testament to his versatility as a pianist. The interplay between Barron, Washington, and Harris was tight and responsive, demonstrating their shared understanding of and commitment to the music.

The concert concluded with a smooth, cool, and sophisticated performance of Miles Davis’ “All Blues.” Again, Barron’s subtle genius was evident in every note, making this performance a memorable experience for all in attendance.

Miles Davis, by Oliver Nurock @ ohjaygee Johannesburg: Cape Town, South Africa, CC BY 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

The trio’s rendition of “All Blues” was a fitting denouement to an evening that balanced technical brilliance with soulful expression. It also exemplified the trio’s chemistry and Barron’s virtuosic command of jazz tradition.

Barron’s soloing effortlessly weaved through the tune’s modal landscape. Washington’s solo work and bass lines were eloquent and effervescent, while Harris’s drumming was dynamic with confidence and power. The trio’s perfect rendition of “All Blues” honored the moods, colors, and allusions of Davis’ assiduously crafted idiom.

The show is about 60 minutes long, with 7 and 9 pm sets.

Outside view of Smoke Jazz Club. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Kenny Barron Trio at Smoke Jazz

Kenny Barron – Piano
Peter Washington – Bass
Savannah Harris – Drums

Smoke Jazz Club

2751 Broadway
New York, NY 10025

title.rendered: Gabrielle Stravelli and the Brian Newman Band at the Midnight Theatre

content.rendered:
NEW YORK – Gabrielle Stravelli & the Brian Newman Band at the Midnight Theatre

This week, jazz artist Gabrielle Stravelli and four members of the Brian Newman Band presented a fabulous show at the Midnight Theatre a few steps from Hudson Yards in Manhattan, a unique, chic, intimate venue. The theater is softly and colorfully lit to create a cozy and sophisticated atmosphere. It’s a perfect venue for a celebration of jazz artistry, with its décor of plush seating, elegant dining, well-managed ambient lighting and sound, and an inviting atmosphere for a comfortable, engaged audience.

Grammy Award-winning pianist Alex Smith with Gabrielle Stravelli at the Midnight Theatre. Courtesy alexsmithkeys.com

Tonight, nearly two hours of continuous music went by in a moment! I’ll talk about a few tunes and features.

The show began with lights focused on the lovely vocalist and songwriter Gabrielle Stravelli, who took center stage. The accomplished jazz singer, known for her rich, expressive voice and versatility, opened the night with an exciting up-swing version of I Love Being Here With You. Stravelli immediately projected the sophistication, confidence, elegance, and style her followers have come to expect. Her expressive eyes shined with warmth and passion, reflecting her deep connections to the music.

Bassist Steve Whipple with Gabrielle Stravelli at the Midnight Theatre. Courtesy stevenshinjiwhipple.com

From the onset, it was clear that five accomplished jazz artists were on stage, all capable of driving the performance of various songs and styles with creative artistic energy.

Stravelli led the band through a bossa version of Watch What Happens and an up-swing Old Devil Moon. She masterfully navigated structures with impeccable rhythmic accuracy and melodic flexibility, adjusting her vocal intensity to match the rhythmic grooves.

Gabrielle Stravelli with four members of the Brian Newman Band at the Midnight Theatre. Courtesy gabriellestravelli.com

The concert featured tributes honoring legendary writers and performers like Bob Dorough, Karen Carpenter, Ella Fitzgerald, and Mel Tormé. Stravelli’s up-swing interpretation of Dorough’s Devil May Care was playful and whimsical, perfectly capturing the song’s carefree spirit. Her charisma drew the audience as she seamlessly shifted into a rich ballad style in Love Came on Stealthy Fingers, where her delicate phrasing highlighted Dorough’s work’s lyrical, romantic poetry.

Stravelli performed with a stellar jazz quartet, including Grammy Award-winning pianist Alex Smith, drummer and composer Ross Pederson, composer and bassist Steve Whipple, and composer tenor saxophonist Steve Kortyka. With the power of this ensemble, Stravelli ably honored the unmatched artistry of tonight’s featured songs and composers.

Steve Kortyka, Tenor Saxophonist with Gabrielle Stravelli at the Midnight Theater. Photo by bfreedphoto

Performing Just in Time, Stravelli again displayed her vocal scatting agility and dynamic range, reminiscent of Fitzgerald’s signature style, while making the song her own. The band’s tight rhythm section supported Stravelli with a vibrant, swinging backdrop, allowing her voice to soar, eliciting waves of applause and admiration from the audience.

As the evening progressed, Stravelli channeled the improvisational genius of J.J. Johnson in a rendition of Like Someone in Love. Her fluid and inventive scatting echoed the mastery of the late trombonist, and Kortyka’s tenor saxophone complemented her improvisations with smooth, lyrical lines.

Drummer Ross Pederson with Gabrielle Stravelli at the Midnight Theatre. Photo by Will Adamy

The mood shifted to heartfelt nostalgia as Stravelli interpreted Close to You, an homage to Karen Carpenter’s tender pathos. Her voice softened, conveying the emotional depth and purity that Carpenter was known for, while the quartet provided a gentle, supportive arrangement highlighting the song’s poignant lyrics. Stravelli’s version of This Masquerade, another tribute to Karen Carpenter, was mesmerizing.

Stravelli channeled the cool, elegant panache of Mel Tormé with Born to Be Blue. Her smooth, velvety tone, combined with the quartet’s refined, understated accompaniment, captured the essence of Tormé’s sophisticated style. The performance left the audience spellbound with its perfect blend of technical skill, emotional depth, and genuine invention.

After a standing ovation and extended accolades, Stravelli performed an encore to wrap up a perfect night of music.

On stage, Gabrielle Stravelli radiated energy and passion. She moved with fluidity and grace, engaging with her band members and the audience, often punctuating her performance with a playful smile or a knowing glance. She traded licks and soloed in par with the splendid quartet. Her rich, versatile voice effortlessly shifted from sultry low notes to powerful highs, each delivered with precision and emotion. She’s not just a singer and jazz artist extraordinaire but a storyteller, bringing each song to life with dynamic phrasing and impeccable timing. Stravelli embodies the perfect balance of elegance and dynamism and is a force to be reckoned with in jazz.

The Midnight Theatre. Courtesy midnighttheatre.com

Be sure to follow Gabrielle Stravelli and see her when you can. She’s in demand and performs at clubs like Chelsea Table + Stage,  Birdland, Dizzy’s Club NYC, The Jazz Cellar, Jazz at Dock’s, Aman NYC, and internationally, so you’ll need to move quickly to catch her next appearance. You can follow her on BandsInTown.

I’m looking forward to Gabrielle Stravelli’s next studio recordings. At the bottom of this article is a link to Dream Dancing from her eponymous album.

Gabrielle Stravelli & the Brian Newman Band at the Midnight Theatre

Midnight Theatre

75 Manhattan Plaza
New York, NY 10001
For Tickets and Information

Readers may also enjoy our reviews of Laura and Linda Benanti: Mothers Know Best at 54 Below, John Pizzarelli and the Swing 7 at Birdland, Adam Pascal and Anthony Rapp: Celebrating Friendship and History, Yachtly Crew, Opera in the Garden by ON SITE OPERA, Norm Lewis at 54 Below, Tony Danza, Meg Okura at the Met Museum, Laura Benanti at the Minetta Lane Theater, Brazilian Jazz at Le Bab Ilo in Paris, and Marilyn Maye birthday celebration at 54 Below.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall
As the clock ticks to the opening time of this play, Tom (Damian Young) steps onto the [platform stage from behind a layer of plastic curtain reminiscent of the kind used in restaurant at the entrance toad walk-in refrigerator.  Hmmn.  Tom fusses with very important guy stuff: his cuffs, his phone, his jacket placed just so on his chair.  Soon Nell (Alison Cimmet) enters and brings a chill of her own.  She takes a chair from the stack awkwardly placed upstage, climbs over Tom and sets hers down as far away as she can get and still be in the same room.  Neither speaks or acknowledges.  Little by little, giving time for their predecessors to have their own bits of predictable business, the rest of the crew dribbles in.  Jude (Delia Cunningham) arrives with apology written all over her.  Julian (Marcus Gladney Jr. ) bops in hiding behind his earphones.  Evelyn (Gamze Ceylan) rushes in feeling as hot as Nell is cold.  Bringing up the rear is Lily (Ana Cruz Kayne) who nearly trips over her own self absorption.
The set-up, we discover early on, is that this is a support group, and everyone has shown up on time except for one person – Beth.  Beth is the leader.  Without her this group is adrift big time.
But the real kicker is this: a quick glance at the program will tell you that there are six actors listed in the program.  A quick glance at the stage will confirm that there are six actors on the stage.
Ergo – Beth the Leader is not coming today or tomorrow or ever.
The question is – why bother with the play if the plot has no legs?  I have been to shows at which programs were not handed out until the audience was leaving the theatre.  Seems like that would have been an appropriate solution.
Once we realize that Beth is a no-show, we are faced with the dilemma of why bother sticking around the theatre.  More important – why do these characters (who don’t know what we know) stay in the claustrophobic and poorly lit room for their entire meeting time.  I once took a class where the instructor led us through the importance of keeping a character in the room.  What does the writer have to do.  and what do the other characters have to do?
These actors did everything they could to lift this play up. Their timing was spot on.  They were invested in the story and the text. There were moments of delicious black humor, moments of insensitivity, moments of vulnerable joy.  But the moments never added up to create a whole.   The characters stayed insulated in their worlds, only emerging when it was time to further their own personal tales. Their predicaments are each rolled out in fairly predictable and evenly balanced revelations.  This is a grief group, and everyone has a sad story to tell.  In fact, some of these tales are compelling – especially the simplest ones.  Grief is grief, after all, and the exploration of its effects on “ordinary” lives never gets old.
Unlike this play, in which no one was given a chance to be spectacular.  This play missed the author’s intentions by a yard and got old very, very fast.
Of course the audience gave them a standing ovation.  Of course.
SOMEONE SPECTACULAR by Doménica Feraud, Directed by Tatiana Pandiani.
WITH Gamze Ceylan,  Alison Cimmet, Delia Cunningham, Marcus Gladney Jr., Ana Cruz Kayne, and Damian Young.
Scenic design is by dots, costume design is by Siena Zoë Allen (Broadway, lighting design is by Oona Curley and sound design is by Tony Award nominee Mikaal Sulaiman.
At The Romulus Linney Courtyard Theatre at The Pershing Square Signature Center (480 West 42 Street, Jim Houghton Way).
Through September 7. Tickets HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

Sutton Foster is out of this world fantastic in the new adaptation of Once Upon A Mattress by Amy Sherman-Palladino. She is an indescribably stunning comedic actress and musical goddess. She sits on the same heavenly cloud along with Carol Burnett, Debbie Reynolds,Lucille Ball and Ethel Merman.

But she is not alone.

Michael Urie,  fabulous comedic performer, is the perfect Prince Dauntless.

The two of them tear the stage up with their immense abilities at slapstick, their incredible vocal mastery, their hilarious creations of Winnifred the Hopeful and Prince Dauntless the Desperate.

They are joined by Daniel Breaker as the Jester, our narrator, Brooks Ashmanskas as the Wizard, Ana Gasteyer as Queen Aggravain, David Patrick Kelly as the silent but deadly hilarious King Sextimus the Silent, and Will Chase whose Sir Harry almost steals the show along with Nikki Renee Daniels’ Lady Larken.

The story is based on the Hans Christian Anderson short story The Princess and the Pea.

The musical first premiered in 1959 with music by Mary Rodgers, lyrics by Marshall Barer, and book by Jay Thompson, Dean Fuller, and Marshall Barer.

Queen Aggravain doesn’t want to give up her position as head of the household and Kingdom. The rules state that when her son, the Prince, marries she will have to resign as head of both household and Kingdom, or in her case Queendom. To keep herself in power she has created a convoluted notion of what a true Princess is and puts to the test every Princess who is looking for the prince’s hand in marriage. The test is a plethora of ridiculous questions that she and her wizard have created. The Queen has also passed a law that, until the Prince marries, no one in the kingdom shall marry. It’s been years and everyone in the kingdom wants to get married. Two we know of have secretly fallen in love, Sir Harry and Lady Larken, and unfortunately for them are now pregnant. They NEED Prince Dauntless to marry asap. ASAP! So, Sir Harry takes off on his trusty steed to a far off land to find a suitable princess. He finds Princess Winnifred from the swampy muddy part of the world. Winnifred and Dauntless, two of the most awkward humans on the planet, fall instantly for one another, but the Queen will have none of it. The test for Winnifred will be the hardest of them all. One pea at the bottom of twenty mattresses. If Winnifred is able to sleep on the mattresses then she will be sent away and the hunt for a Princess suitable for Dauntless will continue as only a true princess would be sensitive enough to register the lump from the pea and be unable to sleep.

The story, the slapstick, and the wonderful songs had me ear-to-ear smiling. This show is a gem of American musical theater and it is for all audiences. At the matinee I attended were several young children and their laughter filled the theater and had all the adults enraptured not only by the wonderful show before us but by the wonderful pure joy being experienced all around us.

This is, I believe, a must see for any who love Broadway musicals. It is not perfect. The design of the set is baffling, as are the costumes, though Winnifred does enter in a costume that held one unexpected unbelievable surprise after another. Some of the choreography felt dated and stilted, but I believe that may have been due to the limitations of the crowded cumbersome stage.

Nonetheless, there are songs and performances that will touch your heart and have you laughing.

Prince Dauntless’ father, the King (David Patrick Kelly), had a curse put on him that has struck him silent. So when Dauntless asks his father to tell him about marriage and where babies come from in the show stopping number “Man to Man”, let me just say the mime work of Mr. Kelly and the confusion of Prince Dauntless, along with the hilarious (kid friendly) lyrics, had the audience in tears of laughter.

This is the exemplary first theatrical experience for that young person in your life and a great time spent with joy and laughter for you.

Once Upon A Mattress newly adapted by Amy Sherman-Palladino (The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel), directed by Lear deBessonet

With: Sutton Foster, Michael Urie, Brooks Ashmanskas, Daniel Breaker, Will Chase, Nikki Renée Daniels, David Patrick Kelly, Ana Gasteyer

Ensemble: Kara Lindsay, Daniel Beeman,Wendi Bergamini,Cicily Daniels,Taylor Marie Daniel,Ben Davis,Sheldon Henry,Oyoyo Joi, Amanda Lamotte,Sarah Michele Lindsey,Michael Olaribigbe,Adam Roberts,Jeffrey Schecter,Darius Wright,and Richard Riaz Yoder

Choreography by Lorin Latarro; Scenic Design David Zinn; Costume Design Andrea Hood; Lighting Design Justin Townsend; Sound Design by Kai Harada; Hair, Wig and Makeup Design by J. Jared Janas and Physical Comedy and Effects Skylar Fox. Orchestrations by Bruce Coughlin and Mary-Mitchell Campbell will serve as Music Supervisor, with Annbritt du Chateau as Music Director.

The Hudson Theater 141 West 44th Street NY NY 10036

Tickets HERE

Running Time: 2 hours and 15 minutes with one intermission

Once Upon A Mattress runs through November 30. The production is then scheduled to transfer to the Ahmanson Theatre in Los Angeles from December 10, 2024–January 5, 2025
