content.rendered:
By David Walters

Standing over her while she sleeps, this line is Othello’s metaphor for dousing a candle and its parallel in killing Desdemona.

“Put out the light, and then put out the light.”

In his one man show My Own Private Shakespeare there are similar numerous parallels in the lines of the Bard and the tumultuous life lived by the Shakespearean actor Justin Hay. In these lines he seeks solace, comfort in not being alone, and understanding of the tragedies that have befallen him. His father dies that he hasn’t seen in fifteen years leaving much unsaid. His wife blatantly has a relationship with another man entangling his children in the mess. He finds out that he has a brain tumor that needs multiple operations. One is difficult, two is almost bearable, but all three at once is enough for anyone to sink to, “Out, out, brief candle.”

Baring his soul and using the plays Macbeth, Hamlet, Othello, Lear, Richard III, and Caesar, Justin gives us one of the most simple and honest sharings of a life that I have had the pleasure of attending. Even though it’s Shakespeare, there’s no theatricality. Even though it’s Shakespeare, there’s no embellishment. And because it’s Shakespeare it’s the more richer for having gone through it. Over five hundred years ago and there is still so much relevancy to the human experience that we live today. Justin not only finds parallels in the soliloquies, but also in several scenes from those plays, flipping back and forth between characters with alacrity.

A key moment in Justin’s early life is flagged as the starting gun of what he was to become and how he looks at his life and the world, through a Shakespearean lens. He recalls his fourteen year old self listening to a vinyl record of Sir Larry doing Othello, not completely understanding the words and what was being said, but realizing that he was being permanently pierced by the recitation and that he would never be the same. He wasn’t.

The director, Mona Zaidi, has done a marvelous job keeping the tone and pace reigned in, adding to the simplicity of the time of tragedy and trauma experienced by Mr. Hay.

Justin’s play closed on August 4th as it was a small part of Frigid New York‘s Little Shakespeare Festival.  There are many other offerings at the festival to check out.

My Own Private Shakespeare by Justin Hay, featuring select scenes by William Shakespeare, directed by Mona Zaidi.

FRIGID New York’s mission is to provide both emerging and established artists the opportunity to create and produce original work of varied content, form, and style, and to amplify their diverse voices.

title.rendered: Adam Pascal and Anthony Rapp: “Celebrating Friendship and History”

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

If you are a fan of either Adam Pascal or Anthony Rapp or have seen the musical RENT more than once – this is a show intended for your very person.  As it happens I am 33% there.  I am indeed a fan of Anthony Rapp for his television work in Star Trek Discovery in which he played the first openly gay crew member, Lt. Commander Paul Stamets.  I admired the writing on that show, and Rapp brought just the right amount of unpredictability to his role.

As for Mr. Pascal – I was not familiar with his work before this show.

And most importantly – I never saw Jonathan Larzon’s  RENT. Both men were in the original cast.  I didn’t see it downtown at New York Theatre workshop where it premiered in 1986.  I didn’t see it when it moved up to Broadway that same year.  I didn’t see it during its 12 year run that ended in 2008.  I didn’t see the 2005 movie adaptation.

Guilty as charged with no explanation.

But let me tell you – just about everyone in the rambunctious audience I joined last night DID see one or more of these iterations.  And from the sound of their joyful sing-along efforts these folks were soaring with pride as they joined in on all of the six songs Pascal and Rapp selected from the RENT score.  There were a few other songs they grabbed onto as well.

Pascal and Rapp were prepared for this.  Along with their musical director Daniel Weiss (who played in the orchestra for RENT), Lee Moretti (guitar), Paul Gil (Bass), and Jerry Marrotta (Drums) they created a trajectory that featured key musical phrases to alert the audience as to what was coming.  This tight combo loves a good lead-in that will nearly set the audience ablaze.

Anthony Rapp, Adam Pascal; Photo Michael Allan Galvez

Not only do they set us up, and have a fabulous time doing it – they nearly blow us out of the room.  I don’t know how or why it was decided that louder was good and loudest was best.  The musical accompaniment (including Pascal’s guitar) was nothing short of hot and fierce.  The volume was so loud that the lyrics were lost when Pascal and Rapp sang.  The evening felt more like a rock concert – and 54 Below is not suited for that.  There was no let up except for a sprinkling of songs (“I-95” [Collingwood and Schlessinger], “Solsbury Hill” [Peter Gabriel], and “Seasons of Love” [Jonathan Larson].)  Each of these had snatches of lyrics that were understandable.

Like I said – I came into the theatre unarmed.  I was frustrated in the extreme not to understand the lyrics.  For the rest of the audience, however, this did not seem to be a problem, because they knew the songs – or at least the chorus bits like …”525,600 minutes…” and were happy to sing along wherever they could fit in.   All around me folks were rocking out in their seats and bobbing their heads up, down, to and fro.  We sat next to a delightful couple from Ontario who had come into town for birthday celebrations.  They knew RENT pretty much by heart.  For them this evening was awesome.  No question.  I have to say their joy WAS contagious.

Watching Pascal and Rapp reminded me of watching “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” back in the day.  We sure did NOT know all the lyrics to that music, but that didn’t stop us from belting out, “Let’s Do The Time Warp Again” over and over and over.

Like i said – if you are already fans of these gents or of RENT – you have a huge treat in store.

Adam Pascal and Anthony Rapp: “Celebrating Friendship and History”  August 6-10 and 13-17.  TICKETS HERE.

title.rendered: Shrek Jr. at Redhouse Arts Center

content.rendered:
By Eryn Malafronte

Last Friday, I had the pleasure of seeing SHREK JR. at Redhouse Arts Center in Syracuse, NY. The production value and passion of this production were anything but junior.

Imagine having a grand total of 10 days to put on a full production, a concept that would almost certainly terrify any adult actor. Given the challenge, these kids stepped up to the plate, taking on multiple responsibilities (helping construct props, costumes, and learning new skills such as puppetry and stilt walking) apart from developing fully fledged fairy tale characters with unique personalities of their own. This was especially expressed through the choreography by Andrea Dotto, which allowed every ensemble member an opportunity to shine.

The show started with the director, Brendan Malafronte, stepping out onto the elevated black box stage to deliver a speech about cardboard. It sounds unconventional.  The message behind it, however, was clear.  As children, the depths of our imagination and play are limitless, and a cardboard box is anything but a cardboard box. A cardboard box can be a rocket to the moon or a pirate ship sailing on the grand line. It is a vessel to take us into an alternate reality, and that’s exactly the purpose cardboard served for this production.

The show opened with a trio of STORYTELLERS (Emma Mollapour, Will Lavin, and Gavin Lambert) who entered wielding cardboard swords, a cardboard storybook, and a giant pencil. Upon opening the book and putting pencil to page, the ensemble transforms into a choreographed “cardboard tornado,” and we are segued into the swamp of the ornery ogre SHREK (Maxwell Elmer) for the first number of the show, an ensemble piece, “Big Bright Beautiful World.” Shrek, as well as the younger iteration of Shrek,wore a “commedia dell’arte”- like Shrek mask made by Mr. Malafronte. The first ensemble piece gives us a glimpse into the life of a character who is perceived as nothing more than a monster, who then finds themselves inconvenienced when a group of confused, disgruntled fairy tale creatures get evicted from their homes and are forced to seek shelter in the swamp at Shrek’s door (“Story of My Life”). The distinctions between every ensemble character were spectacular.

On a new quest to kick the fairy tale intruders off his property, Shrek is soon joined (by force) by a hilariously charming, mouthy mule, DONKEY (Inri Stitt). Both Elmer and Stitt brought a wonderfully refreshing take on the dynamic duo, whose chemistry left the audience eager to see more from the moment we were introduced. Our new key players are then taken by the Duloc Guards and met by the desperate-to-be king, LORD FARQUAAD (Matt Kelly), who, knowing the perils of rescuing a princess from the tallest tower and a fire-breathing dragon, quickly takes advantage of the newcomers and strikes a deal: a princess for the deed to Shrek’s swamp.

Plenty is to be said about what happens next, the introduction to the not-your-average heroine of the show, who is eager to find her prince and holds a secret of her own: FIONA (Juliet Weber) comes to us in another musical montage featuring the younger versions of Fiona (Kennady Lambert and Rhoda Cateforis), who all delivered with beautiful voices in perfect unison. Shrek scales the tower, and Donkey is left to deal with the fire-breathing dragon. The DRAGON (Tamera Jones), whose powerhouse voice matched her character, is revealed by her number (“Forever”), a song exclusively for the junior version. The DRAGON PUPPETEERS (Olivia Ferrara, Danae Miller, Lucy Ghezzi, Sophia Petrivelli, Elinor Hanlon) were a wonderful surprise. As a professional puppeteer myself, it was amazing to see so many young puppeteers move so fluidly and put in the work to give the dragon so much life and personality, a puppet is only a lifeless doll without the puppeteers, after all. Hats off to Caitlin Friedberg for directing the puppetry in this production, as well as constructing the cardboard, multi-person dragon puppet, even working with the young actors in the show and teaching them how to craft and stilt walk (yes, stilt walk). Amazing puppetry was also seen in GINGY (Rina Miller), who was on par with the hilarious cookie in the movie (Gingy puppet made by Brendan Malafronte).

The newfound trio begins their quest back to Duloc. Through spending time together, Shrek finds out, through developing feelings for Fiona, that maybe it’s not the outside that defines a person’s character but the character of the person themselves. Donkey and Fiona form a bond of secrecy to keep Fiona’s secret from Shrek, and a series of misunderstandings lead to Shrek fighting for Fiona’s heart in a beautiful ballad (“Big Bright Beautiful World”), which Elmer delivered a beautiful, heartfelt rendition of. The show ends with each character on stage for the finale (“This Is Our Story”), which encapsulates the theme of the show: everyone’s story is unique, different, and beautiful, and you are given the power to write your own ending.

SHREK JR. : Was based on the DreamWorks Animation Motion Picture by William Steig. Written by David Lindsay- Abaire, music by Jeanine Tesori, and Directed by Brendan Malafronte.

WITH: STORYTELLERS 1, 2, 3 (Emma Mollapour, Will Lavin, and Gavin Lambert), SHREK (Maxwell Elmer), PRINCESS FIONA (Juliet Weber), DONKEY (Inri Stitt), LORD FARQUAAD (Matt Kelly), MAMA OGRE (Aadya Singh), PAPA OGRE (Amaar Bhan Ahangar), YOUNG FIONA/YOUNG SHREK (Kennady Lambert), TEEN FIONA (Rhoda Cateforis), PIGS 1, 2, 3 (Arden Williams, Mila Green, Italy Glover), DRAGON (Tamera Jones), DRAGON PUPPETEERS (Olivia Ferrara, Danae Miller, Lucy Ghezzi, Sophia Petrivelli, Elinor Hanlon), CAPTAIN OF THE GUARDS/PUSS IN BOOTS (Abhay Singh), PINOCCHIO (Olivia Ferrara), BIG BAD WOLF/DULOC MASCOT (Marshall Kania), WICKED WITCH (Elizabeth Plouffe), UGLY DUCKLING/PIED PIPER (Vincenzo Mangan), PETER PAN (Danae Miller), MAMA BEAR (Ruby Toombs), PAPA BEAR (Gus D’Eredita), BABY BEAR (Kate Spencer), GINGY (Rina Miller), BISHOP (Elinor Hanlon), DWARF (Calvin Mele), ROOSTER (Grace Vann), DEER (Noelle Felder), STILTERS (Lucy Ghezzi, Elizabeth Plouffe, Amaar Bhan Ahangar), KNIGHTS (Arden Williams, Mila Green, Italy Glover, Aadya Singh), MORNING PERSON RATS (Arden Williams, Mila Green, Italy Glover, Olivia Ferrara, Aadya Singh, Kate Spencer, Tamera Jones), DULOC GUARDS (Luke Baker, Calvin Mele, Amaar Bhan Ahangar), DULOC DANCERS (Grace Vann, Kennady Lambert, Rhoda Cateforis, Noelle Felder, Aadya Singh, Lucy Ghezzi, Sophia Petrivelli, Elinor Hanlon), DRAGON FIREBALLS (Amaar Bhan Ahangar, Abhay Singh).

Choreography by Andrea Dotto, music direction by Tyler Eighmey, and puppetry direction by Caitlin Friedberg.

Shrek JR. ended its run on July 19th, but future shows at this venue can be seen at the Redhouse Arts Center (315) 362-2785 in Syracuse, NY.

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

A couple of guys taking jabs at each other despite their friendship has always been good for a laugh. The fraternity of such classic comedy duos runs the gamut from Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis to The Odd Couple to The Smothers Brothers to Cheech and Chong. Normally not included on the list, and for good reason, are the team of Ross Cellino and Steve Barnes. Two lawyers from Buffalo, they were not so much hilarious as they were litigious. But, as portrayed by Eric William Morris and Noah Weisberg in the outlandishly entertaining Cellino V. Barnes, there is good reason to add them to the pantheon of grown men behaving childishly in the pursuit of cracking up an audience.

If you had slipped on the ice or been side-swiped at an intersection between the years 1998 and 2020, chances are you’ve heard of, or even hired, Cellino & Barnes. With offices across New York State, they turned the world of personal injury law upside down by spending millions on self-promotion via radio,TV and billboard advertising. They succeeded not so much by being victorious (though they often were), but by being first to mind for anyone needing a lawyer in a hurry.

Directed by Wesley Taylor and Alex Wyse, this 80-minute, occasionally true to life biographical farce had its initial run in Brooklyn in 2018 with the show’s writers, Michael Breen and David Rafailedes, in the title roles. Now, with Morris and Weisberg at the helm, the production is a high energy romp with many a guilty pleasure.

The action begins back when Cellino was working at his father’s law firm, Cellino & Likoudis, and tasked with interviewing a new hire, Barnes. Though Barnes is a step ahead of him all the way, it is Cellino who acts more like the alpha dog, even literally sniffing Barnes before ultimately declaring him a “creepy little genius.” Taking advantage of Barnes’s work ethic and loyalty, Cellino focuses more on being a promoter, creating their own little law firm while still within the confines of his father’s larger one, right up until daddy crushes his son’s confidence and gives them the boot.

Of course, Cellino’s biggest contribution during this time would be the jingle that became ubiquitous and remains a well-worn earworm to this day. As offered up here, the tune comes to Cellino in a moment of divine inspiration, the music and simple words emanating from his body as if he were a man possessed. The ditty is repeated throughout the night to fine comic effect, usually with the words altered to fit the scene at hand. Claiming to be working class rather than the millionaires they are, they warble, “Cellino and Barnes, our take-home isn’t that much. 800-888-8888.”

The dynamic between the two men grows multi-faceted over time. Adversarial one second, then very nearly romantic; tolerant coworkers become best buddies become frenemies. But the music stops when Cellino gets caught using their law firm’s cash in the loan sharking side hustle that Barnes always knew about but chose to ignore. They go their separate ways, the ampersand that bonded them giving way to individual companies, Cellino Law and the Barnes Firm. The ending stays light, not delving into Barnes’s 2020 death in a private plane accident. 

As Barnes, Weisberg’s mannerisms and facial features bring to mind a young Chevy Chase, even with him wearing a bald cap, and is a perfect foil to Morris’s wild-eyed Cellino who becomes so emphatically silly that at one point he claims that he regularly disguises himself to play on his daughter’s hockey team, “Jeanna’s twelve-and-under team needs an enforcer and it takes six-hours of prosthetic makeup to make me a believable little girl.” Clearly the writers aren’t beyond taking a risk or two in the name of a chuckle, or bending facts to speed up the pacing. After all, what could anyone do about it? Sue?

 

Cellino V. Barnes – Written by Mike B. Breen & David Rafailedes; directed by Wesley Taylor & Alex Wyse. 

WITH:  Eric William Morris as Ross Cellino and Noah Weisberg as Steve Barnes.

Scenic and props design by Riw Rakkulchon, costume design by Ricky Lurie, sound design by UptownWorks, and lighting design by Aiden Bezark. Mix and Match Productions at Asylum NYC, 123 E 24th St., 212.203.5435, https://www.cellino-v-barnes.com. Through October 13. Running time: 80 minutes

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

The Meeting: The Interpreter, written by Catherine Gropper purports to examine issues of identity and individual freedom in the face of government’s impersonal, all-powerful machinery.  Gropper was inspired to write this piece after a chance encounter with the interpreter who had done the simultaneous Russian/English translating between the Trump political team and a Russian lawyer during a key meeting in 2016, which subsequently gave rise to various investigations regarding the Russian interference (in Trump’s favor) that occurred in the run-up to the 2016 election.  With such tantalizing subject matter, I was hoping for something a bit Ipcress File or Frost/Nixon, but unfortunately what we got was more Monty Python, without the wit.  The production has well executed art direction and good actors – what’s missing is a play.

I don’t understand why Gropper chose to have only two actors attempt to tell a story involving numerous players.  Having two people wear (literally) so many hats does no one any favors.  The audience is forced to spend so much time trying to figure out what character is talking at any given moment you miss what they’re saying.  And then when we hear what they are saying, the verbiage is so stilted it becomes unbearable.  Why would a playwright choose to spend pages and pages of script quoting from Congressional transcripts, including mind-numbingly pointless procedural instruction?

The decision to use movie clips and live video as an added layer in the storytelling can really enhance a production, when it is done well.  In 2022 the Met Opera put on a daring production of Lucia di Lammermoor, reset in the impoverished American rust belt, in which the director utilized a film screen positioned above the stage on which both film clips and real-time video were projected.  A Steadicam operator followed the action at certain moments, offering a novel close-up of, say, a love duet or a menacing confrontation.  Seeing the same moment from two different angles simultaneously added texture to the storytelling.  However, the Met is a 3,800 seat house with a huge stage.  St. Clements is a tiny theater.  To take up half of the stage with a floor-to-ceiling movie screen, and to place it downstage at the proscenium edge, beside the action rather than hanging it from above, makes absolutely no sense.  Audience Right is faced with this huge screen squarely in front of them, like 10 feet away, and they have to crane their necks to see the actors in the playing space on the other side of the stage.  Audience Left is forced to watch the video screen Audience Right from a position of parallax.  Congratulations.  You have now split a small theater into two even smaller theaters, and almost everyone has a bad seat.

We are left to wonder if this screen will move and we’ll get to see what’s behind it.  (Note:  it doesn’t and we don’t.)  Of course what’s metaphorically ‘behind’ it is the action taking place in what’s left of the stage once the screen moves from center to its ‘home’ at Audience Right.  To further crop the playing space by encircling it fully with the track for the video camera dolly, thereby trapping the actors within a small, spare, sterile set, is just weird.  The audience is barred entry at every turn.  Kelley Curran and Frank Wood sit behind a desk, stand in a glassed-in sound booth at the back of the stage, spin desk chairs, run around stage.  And then one of them will appear in super close-up on the video screen.  It is either too far or way too close, but regardless, it adds up to a big ‘keep out’ sign.

Curran and Wood are clearly excellent actors, but their talents are wasted here.  Burdened by the pointless business of their onstage action (Why is Curran staple-gunning her neckties to a box?  Why is Wood tap dancing?  What is up with the apple?) and impeded by the continual interruption of the video camera rolling on by, they cannot win.  Here’s an idea:  get out of the way and let the actors act.

The writing does nothing to further a narrative.  It offers no basis on which to understand the increasingly bizarre behavior of the characters. They snap their fingers and bang on the table – why?  Nothing ever feels natural about how they express themselves.  They’re either declaiming or having self-consciously Meaningful Conversation.  Yet, for all the talking, very little storytelling takes place.

Puppets, live video, sound, projections, movie clips, random arm gestures  — I’m sure it all felt really cool in rehearsal, but someone needed to step outside the studio bubble and actually look at the overworked, chaotic product of their experimentation.  So much effort has been taken to drain this material of any humanity.  I mean, international intrigue, espionage, money laundering, torture, and the very real imperilment of the U.S. democracy, and we get creepy puppets and interpretive dance.  Seriously?

I’m sorry to be so harsh, but this production left me at a total loss.  And I was not alone.

The Meeting: The Interpreter, written by Catherine Gropper and directed by Brian Mertes.  Starring Kelley Curran and Frank Wood.

Set Designer Jim Findlay; Projection Designer Yana Biryukova; Costume Designer Olivera Gajicis; Lighting Designer Barbara Samuels; Composer and Sound Designer Dan Baker; Puppet Designer and Builder Julian Crouch; Videographer Tatiana Stolporskaya,

Runs July 29 – August 25 at the Theatre at St. Clements (423 W 46th St., NYC)  For tickets go to www.meetinginterpreterplay.com.  Run time 90 minutes, no intermission.

excerpt.rendered: The Meeting: The Interpreter, purports to examine issues of identity and individual freedom in the face of government’s impersonal, all-powerful machinery. Sadly, the play fails to communicate the urgency or the human toll of high-stakes political machinations. With all of the multi-media distractions, so much effort has been taken to drain this material of any humanity.  I mean, international intrigue, espionage, money laundering, torture, and the very real imperilment of the U.S. democracy, and we get creepy puppets and interpretive dance.  Seriously?

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

It is a good thing that JOB, by Max Wolfe Friedlich, is at the Helen Hayes Theatre.  The Hayes is next to Sardi’s.  Sardi’s is where you want to go after you see this show because you will need to debrief.  Don’t just toodle off home without having a drink (alcohol or mocktail)  and chatting with your theatre companion.  If by chance you have no companion go in anyway because Jeremy, the upstairs bartender, has definite opinions on the conclusion of JOB.  You can debrief with him.

It is rare that I have the privilege to see and review a production more than once.  And when I have, it was certainly not a two-hander.  Lucky for me, I got this opportunity with JOB.  Because not only did I get to admire the intricacies of Friedlich’s writing, I got to witness this pas de deux between Peter Friedman and Sydney Lemmon.  Talk about a study in acting.

The time is January 2020. We all remember that January…  Location is outside of Silicon Valley.   Jane (Lemmon) has had a few emotional issues, okay a certified meltdown,  while on the job at a big tech company (We are told we know the one, but do we? Google is owned by Alphabet, who also owns FitBit and Waze.  Facebook is now Meta and owns Instagram and What’s App.  Even as we speak there are start-ups starting up and being bought.).  Jane’s meltdown went viral, and she has been suspended from her job until she gets the all clear from a therapist.  Lloyd (Friedman) is the therapist of choice, presumably hired by Jane’s company.  Lloyd is the patron therapist of lost causes.  He tells Jane that he is the best.

Jane’s job at the unnamed company is to ferret out objectionable posts on the Internet and banish them to Hell.  But each time she does a piece of her goes along for the ride, so that by the time we meet her there is little of Jane left.  By objectionable I do not mean “in bad taste.” I mean the kind of videos that are violent in ways we cannot imagine.  Jane wants her job back because she is the line of defense.  She tells Lloyd, “The internet isn’t some fringe “young people” thing anymore – it’s where we live. It’s our home and I am the front line of defense – there’s nobody else. All of the worst things in the world come right to my computer screen.”

Did I mention the gun?

No secret as we see it right away.  And while Jane agrees to put it away in her flimsy cloth bag, we never forget it is there.  Neither does Lloyd.  It is the gun that tips the scales and makes Lloyd a hostage.  One could argue that he has plenty of time to dash out the door, but the action is so fast, and Jane so nimble that the image of them going toe to toe is not out of reach.

As it is, Jane more or less takes over Lloyd’s office, moving furniture, clearing off an end table to make into a seat.  Jane bears the weight of the text as she scrambles to get enough of her thought process and circumstances out so that Lloyd will write the words that will give her her job back.  Either that or, well, you know.awhileLloyd, on the other hand, must listen.  And Friedman is a damn good listener.  Lloyd must unravel this Rubrics Cube of a person who speaks in code.  He has to dip in like a laser surgeon and get out before Jane has time to lunge like a feral cat.  Her life depends on it, and so may his.  Which is why the choice for  Jane to give her two most important monologues to us instead of Lloyd was a mystery.  We are depending on Lloyd to keep us grounded.  We get our cues from  his reactions.  When the focus is entirely on Jane we are lost.  It takes us awhile to get righted again.  Unfortunate.

The dialogue here is like a tennis match on steroids.  Just when you think there is a point made, an invisible umpire calls “foul” and you are back to an even score.  Lloyd is the solid place against which Jane hurls her whole self.  Without Lloyd there would be no Jane.  She would burst into flame and disappear.

Even as the story winds up, the game piles high with Aces and match points until the stakes become life and death.

While the text is often lumpy and filled with switchbacks, the superb performances of Friedman and Lemmon are the centerboard on this vessel.  Friedman’s text allows us to fasten ourselves to the whirlpool that is their relationship.  We stay there until we are asked to disembark with a final scene that leaves us gasping.

Tell Jeremy we sent you.

JOB  by Max Wolf Friedlich, directed by Michael Herwitz

WITH Peter Friedman Sydney Lemmon.

Scenic design by Scott Penner, costume design by Michelle J. Li, lighting design by Mextly Couzin, sound design by Cody Spencer, and original music by Devonté Hynes.

At The Helen Hayes Theater.  Through September 29.  Tickets HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: It’s Not What It Looks Like

content.rendered:
By David Walters

One of the most refreshing things about It’s Not What It Looks Like, now playing at Soho Playhouse, is that it’s a tale of two cousins, male and female, dealing with what life has dropped on them. That relationship is not often explored which makes this story and its telling stand out as well as adding a new depth of character relationship now that the sex has been taken out.  This leaves an open space to explore the play’s themes of lying to self, grief, and are any of us good people (probably not).

The writers are also its stars (John Collins (head writer) as the character M (reminds me of a young Timothy Hutton and just as compelling), and Chesney Mitchell (writing collaborator) (brings deep caring and frustration to the relationship) as the character W. This duel role as writers and actors gives them both a thorough understanding of their characters and this comes across in their dynamite acting which is able to gloss over the little weaknesses in the script and provide a very satisfying evening of good actors telling a compelling story through flawed but deeply human characters.

The story begins at the crescendo of the play where a life and death event has just happened and they are caught with blood on their hands. The characters feel caught in the act and have a compelling need to justify their actions, wanting to grant absolution for what led them to this situation. With direct audience address and a minimum of production value (two chairs and a projection screen), the scenes then flip back and forth over the course of the past year.  These scenes illuminate moments and interactions that don’t necessarily bring them solace about their mistakes along the way, but does grant them clarity about their misjudgments. The strength in this play (as in all good stories) lies in the relationship that’s been built between John and Chesney and how their characters hurt and heal each other.

W: I’m always gonna worry about you. You know that.

M: And I’m always going to want to apologize to you. (slight pause)

W: I think that’s just the way it goes.

It’s Not What It Looks Like is well worth your time and the ticket price.  $36.00

—–

It’s Not What It Looks Like was the winner of the 2023 Soho Playhouse Lighthouse Series.

Written by John Collins, directed by Vincent DeGeorge, and in collaboration with Chesney Mitchell.

The production team includes Nicholas Pollock (Lighting Design).

Now through August 10th at Soho Playhouse, 15 Vandam St. New York, NY 10013

excerpt.rendered: A very satisfying evening of good actors telling a compelling story of flawed but deeply human characters.

@graph.description: 57 years of lovingly working on the craft of theater, what it is, what it means to create it, as well as the diligent process involved in its birthing, has led me to act, write, produce, work every job on crew, and watch from the audience a multitudinous array of offerings that loosely define the word theater. I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

In Re:CREATION,  playing at the Joyce Theater,  the avant-garde dance company Pilobolus is creating some real magic.  The work consists of two programs: Program A, Dreams and Program B, Memory, playing in repertory on alternate dates until August 11th.  I attended Memory on Wednesday night, and all I can say is wow.  It was a performance of affecting beauty, lyricism and daring.  Everything falls into place in the five individual pieces that comprise this program – exuberant dance, intricate, sweeping choreography, literate and at times deeply personal lighting design, and costumes that perfectly encapsulate the substance of each work.

The first dance, Untitled, is the most recognizably narrative piece.   Two women in billowing skirts playfully flutter around stage, as if chasing each other in a summer garden.  They unexpectedly rise up as on stilts, to stand imposingly on high.  Their ‘stilts’, we discover, are men —  two children of Eden in their birthday suits.  The choreography, a seeming meditation on innocence and age, is beautiful and very human.  In the second work, Behind the Shadows, Pilobolus reverts to its trademark shadow dance technique, where whimsical silhouettes morph behind a scrim (think shadow puppets, writ large).  The rolling of the scrim about the stage creates a “now you see me; now you don’t” effect, as we are literally given a peek behind the curtain, revealing what goes on behind the scenes in the creatioon of whimsy.  With its groovy 60’s beat and vibrant playfulness, Behind the Shadows extends its welcoming energy to the audience, inviting us to the party.

In a dramatic metaphysical shift, the next piece, Noctuary takes us to the surreal world of dreams.  Where do go when we close our eyes?  What unseen forces drive us?  What unbidden creatures visit?  The choreography is deceptively athletic, as its vigor is sublimated to weightless lifts and consistent, intentional lines.  In gestures both narrative and abstract, the dancers silently investigate tension, loss and reunion. 

The second half of the evening drew us deeper into dream – straight down to the Underworld and its complement of surreal, ephemeral, mysterious characters.  Tales from the Underworld casts a spell, as choreographic and visual sleight-of-hand builds illusion on illusion.  Ghostly apparitions, billowing fabric add to the magic, as dancers appear to spin overhead unaided or are swallowed by the darkness.  From flying creatures to Earthly inhabitants, the last piece, Branches takes us the African Savannah.  The dancers portray various animals gathering at a watering hole.  Their verisimilitude is uncanny.  I don’t know about anyone else, but I definitely saw some Meerkats.   Fluid, funny, playful gesture, to the accompaniment of birdsong and rustling leaves created harmony that washed over us like a welcome sigh.  The audience was on its feet within seconds of the curtain closing.

So often modern choreography is mechanical and distant, an intellectual exercise at bests and an artistic failure at worst.  With Pilobolus it is just the opposite.  This company thrives on connection.  In the hands (and arms and legs and torsos) of these extraordinary dancers (a/k/a the fittest human beings on the planet), any choreography blooms with color and possibility.  Connor Chaparro, Quincy Ellis, Marlon Feliz, Hannah Klinkman, Sean Langford and Derion Loman glide, spin and leap in a performance of breathtaking virtuosity which nonetheless paints effortlessly within the lines.  It’s nothing short of stunning.  You really don’t want to miss this magical mystery tour-de-force.

re:CREATION at  The Joyce Theater (175 Eighth Avenue, at 19 Street) through August 11, 2024.  Matinees at 2:00pm; evening performances 7:30pm weekdays and 8:00pm weekends.  For Tickets go to www.joyce.org.  Run time: two hours with one intermission.

excerpt.rendered: Pilobolus, the storied, avant-garde dance company formed in 1971 by three inquisitive Dartmouth students has evolved into a major driver of change in the dance world — and for good reason.  They are sui generis, in style and inventiveness.  Pilobolus is known for ‘how did they do that?’ – a quality well in evidence in re:CREATION.  The choreographic sleight of hand, and the effortlessness with which it is performed, is nothing short of stunning.  You really don’t want to miss this magical mystery tour-de-force.  Hurry! You only have until August 11th.

title.rendered: The Sabbath Girl: A New Musical

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

Back in 2020, the Penguin Rep Theatre, a 45-year-old non-profit based in Stony Point, NY, brought Cary Gitter’s romantic comedy, The Sabbath Girl, to the 59E59 Theaters for a three week run. Spurred on by Penguin’s artistic director, Joe Brancato, the play now boasts an impressive score and returns to the venue reincarnated as The Sabbath Girl: A New Musical. Indeed, transformation is at the heart of the matter in this pleasing production as a young couple move away from their past, lonely lives and into each other’s arms.

The entire enterprise is as sweet as a glass of Manischewitz, minus the cloying aftertaste. The show is so winningly sung by its capable five-member cast and so lovingly directed by Brancato, one cannot help but be wooed by its charms, despite a final scene that is so never in doubt. Given today’s turbulent times, there is a lot to be said for the escapist comforts of a predictable ending.

Angie (Marilyn Caserta) is an Italian American 30-year-old from New Jersey, proud of her independence and focused solely on running a successful downtown art gallery. As she explains to her grandmother, Sophia (Diana DiMarzio), “Happy can wait. I have work to do. Artists to discover, shows to plan.” Fate, of course, has other plans for her. 

She is one week into living in her new Manhattan apartment when there is a knock on the door. It is her neighbor from down the hall, Seth (Max Wolkowitz). Seth is an Orthodox Jew with a problem. Well, several problems, but the most urgent being that it is the Sabbath, a time when the observant are forbidden to do any type of work, including turning on appliances. He asks Angie if she wouldn’t mind turning on his air conditioner for him. It is not so much a fiery meet cute as it is a cautious howdy-do, but a spark is lit nonetheless and it won’t be long till the two turn hot and heavy midway through lighting the Sabbath candles.

There is no shortage of obstacles and distractions on their way to true love, starting with Seth’s faith. On one hand he is a pretty unorthodox Orthodox, divorced from a wife he did not love and separated from his Riverdale congregation. And though his job as a knish shop owner is as old school as it gets, he embraces contemporary society via experimental knish flavors like pineapple, or jalapeno and cheddar. Still, the weight of dating a religious outsider nags at him, as does his judgmental sister, Rachel (Lauren Singerman), who does her best to lure him back to the flock of available Semites.

Angie, meanwhile, thinks she might be better off with Blake (Rory Max Kaplan), an egotistical artist in dark sunglasses who offers, in the most double-entendre-esque way, to paint her. Bad boys have their place but Angie’s better angels bring her to her senses. When she visits Seth’s shop, they share a knish instead of a canoodle, still it is hot. And the sexiest striptease of the night is when Seth removes his yarmulke. “Yeah,” he informs a shocked Angie, “it comes off.”

Caserta is an endearing Angie, torn but never ditzy and offering some powerhouse vocals. Wolkowitz brings a rugged warmth to Seth, avoiding stereotypes on his path to finding a strong voice for his quiet character. The quite funny Kaplan does wonders with unearthing Blake’s hidden depths, while the equally amusing Singerman nudges and needles without turning harsh. And DiMarzio brings a soft glow to Sophia, instilling grandmotherly wisdom along the way (“Rosary beads, prayer shawls: same difference.”).

The music, by Neil Berg, is often entrancing, especially in the daring quintet, “Listen to Your Heart,” with all the characters simultaneously working out their woes. And while the lyrics are sometimes flat-footed (“Don’t be such a fool/Come back to your shul”), the inspired use of a cello in addition to a keyboard in the two-person orchestra provides proper gravitas amid the mishegoss.

 

The Sabbath Girl: A New Musical –  Book by Cary Gitter, lyrics by Neil Berg and Cary Gitter, music by Neil Berg; directed by Joe Brancato.

WITH: Marilyn Caserta (Angie), Diana DiMarzio (Sophia), Rory Max Kaplan (Blake), Lauren Singerman (Rachel) and Max Wolkowitz (Seth).

Christopher and Justin Swader (set design), Gregory Gale (costume design), Jamie Roderick (lighting design), Kwamina Biney (sound design), Buffy Cardoza (properties), Wendy Bobbitt Cavett (musical supervision & arrangements), Matthew Lowy (musical direction), Alex Wise (orchestrations), Ryan Kasprzak (movement consultant). Penguin Rep Theatre at 59E59 Theaters, 59 East 59th St., 646-892-7999, https://www.59e59.org/shows/show-detail/the-sabbath-girl-a-new-musical/. Through September 1. Running time: 90 minutes

title.rendered: OH, MARY! ANNOUNCES EXTENSION  THROUGH NOVEMBER 10, 2024

content.rendered:
For Immediate Release

New York, NY (July 23, 2024) —  Producers Kevin McCollum & Lucas McMahon and Mike Lavoie & Carlee Briglia announced that Oh, Mary! has extended its limited Broadway engagement, and will now run through November 10, 2024.

Tickets for the extension are now on sale via Telecharge or in person at the Lyceum Theatre Box Office. Directed by Tony Award nominee Sam Pinkleton, Oh, Mary! opened to universal critical acclaim on Thursday, July 11, 2024 and was initially scheduled to run through September 15, 2024.

Oh, Mary! stars Cole Escola (in their Broadway debut) as a miserable, suffocated Mary Todd Lincoln in the weeks leading up to Abraham Lincoln’s assassination. Featuring Conrad Ricamora as Mary’s Husband, James Scully as Mary’s Teacher, Bianca Leigh as Mary’s Chaperone, and Tony Macht as Mary’s Husband’s Assistant, the entire production is directed by Sam Pinkleton. Hannah Solow, Peter Smith and Martin Landry complete the cast.

General tickets, beginning at $49.00, are available now on Telecharge, or in person at the Lyceum Box Office, or by calling 212.239.6200. For more information, go to OhMaryPlay.com. The current performance schedule is as follows: Monday – Wednesday at 7:30 PM, Thursday at 5 PM and 8:30 PM, Friday at 7:30 PM, Saturday at 5 PM and 8:30 PM, with no shows on Sundays. Beginning September 16, the performance schedule will change as follows:  Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at 7:30 PM, Thursdays and Saturdays at 5 PM & 8:30 PM, Sundays at 5 PM, with no shows on Tuesdays. Run time is approximately 80 minutes.

There is a digital lottery and an in-person rush available as follows:

Digital Lottery — Entries for the Oh, Mary! digital lottery will open at 12 AM one day before the performance, and winners are drawn the same day at 10 AM and 3 PM. Winners may buy up to 2 tickets at $47.00 each. Visit OhMaryPlay.com/lottery to enter.

In-Person Rush

‍A limited number of in-person rush tickets will be available at the Lyceum Theatre Box Office (149 West 45th Street) for $43.00, available day-of when the box office opens . Rush ends 30 minutes before curtain. One person may buy up to 2 tickets at $43.00 each.

excerpt.rendered: Watching Oh Mary! is like catching a ride on a runaway stage coach – with no less than six horses…. Cole Escola has created a Mary who is Scarlett O’Hara on uppers.  This Mary is at the center of her own universe, and everyone else is a tiny planet orbiting round her.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Laura and Linda Benanti “Mothers Know Best” at 54 Below though July 24 only

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

I supposed three are sweeter things than watching Laura and Linda Benanti show us (and each other) a good time.  Offhand, nothing comes to mind.  Perhaps that is because I am still basking in the glow of their two-hander ending its current run this evening July 24.  I can only hope for your sake that they will be back.

These two are a tag team of the best order.  They show off what is the core of their musicianship: a boatload of skill and a soupçon of sass.  The musicians who back them are of the same flavor beginning with Music Director Billy Stritch.  Ann Klein on guitar is a lovely surprise.  Steve Doyle on bass and Daniel Glass on drums complete this excellent package.  They turn their opening number “Que Sera Sera” (Livingston and Evans) into a laundry list of things to worry about in the “What Will Be” department (deodorant poisoning and the election are two).  Linda is featured next with two old standards “The Shadow of Your Smile” (Mandel and Webster) and “I had a dream About you” (Maury Yeston) which might have been schmaltz in another person’s hands, but this Benanti put the right tone on both of these songs that were favorites of her parents.

Benanti the Younger returns to the stage wiping her eyes.  “My mother makes me cry,” she tells us just before she directs an audience member to fix his seat position so he doesn’t hurt his neck because that would be upsetting to her.  Sprinkled throughout the night are Benanti stories that reflect the journeys that both of these women continue to experience.  “Wives and Lovers” (Bachrach and David) is turned into a scathing sendup of the confinement of women which was, in a word, exhausting.  The Elder Benati relates the real Covid estate transactions (can we move in Mom?) that brought precious time with grandchildren as they learned new words every day.  This leads to the liquid poetry of “Words” (Maury Yeston).

“Vanilla Ice Cream” (Bock/Harnick) from “She Loves Me” is gifted to us next along with the child in the audience who sent Benanti original drawings that she still has.    Benanti was and is an eclectic mix of qualities that she is feeding out in the wilds of New Jersey.  Life seems to be filled with EVENTS that propel her forward to the next event.  One of those was her encounter with an angel – Chita Rivera – who, during the run of “Nine,” gave over half of her dressing room to Benanti who was recovering from surgery.  Each night as Benenti was singing “Unusual Way” (Maury yeston) to Antonio Banderas she was actually singing to Rivera.

Benanti the Elder follows with “The Man Who Got Away” – a rough and rich tribute to Judy Garland (with a Garland story of course).

“Recovering Ingenue” (Benanti and Almond) is a tribute to both Benanti’s paths that lead them to where they are.  Their penultimate number is a duet of “One More Kiss” that is a soaring investigation of love’s power.

The final “I’m Gonna Miss This,”(Benanti and Klein) is a touching tribute to the spot where these two lives and loves intersect. Sometimes life gives you such rich material you have to put as many stories as you can into a show. The Benanti Duo is rich with tales that hit us where we live.  They are mothers and daughters of each other.  What could be better than that?

Catch them if you can.  Tickets HERE

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

NEW YORK – A Hundred Circling Camps

A Hundred Circling Camps, a world premiere production written by Sam Collier and directed by Rebecca Wear, was an evocative and powerful theatrical experience. Presented by the Dogteam Theatre Project, this production afforded Middlebury College student artists the unique opportunity to perform alongside veteran actors on an Off-Broadway stage, bringing historical struggles to contemporary audiences with compelling resonance. Costumes, lighting, sound, music, and sets were effectively crafted and utilized to maximize dramatic power.

The Ensemble for A Hundred Circling Camps by Sam Collier at the Atlantic Theater Company Stage 2 in New York City. Photo by Clinton Brandhagen

The Great Depression

The play adeptly navigated through pivotal moments in American history, beginning and dealing primarily with the vexing plight of World War I veterans in 1932. While officials initially pledged to pay a “bonus” to veterans in 1945 for their military service in 1918, it was now at the height of the Great Depression when such remuneration would be most welcome.

Fidel Vicioso in a scene from A Hundred Circling Camps by Sam Collier at the Atlantic Theater Company Stage 2 in New York City. Photo by Clinton Brandhagen

The Tombstone Bonus

At the time, veterans called themselves the Bonus Expeditionary Force (BEF) and sardonically described their payment as the “Tombstone Bonus.” You may recall President Herbert Hoover’s reluctance to provide direct federal relief for the needy while emphasizing voluntary action and self-reliance, which were subsequently seen by many as inadequate in the face of the exceptional economic challenges of the time.

Francis Price and Gibson Grimm in a scene from A Hundred Circling Camps by Sam Collier at the Atlantic Theater Company Stage 2 in New York City. Photo by Clinton Brandhagen

This historical narrative was poignantly brought to life through blues, shabby clothes, wooden shanties, and tents, capturing the veterans’ perseverance and the stark realities of their struggle.

Dignity and Justice

The relentless demonstrations and marches by WWI veterans in Washington, D.C., despite their removal with military force, highlighted their obdurate struggle for dignity and justice. This historical chronicle was poignantly brought to life, capturing the veterans’ perseverance and the stark realities of their struggle.

Kayodè Soyemi and Naja Irvin-Conyers in a scene from A Hundred Circling Camps by Sam Collier at the Atlantic Theater Company Stage 2 in New York City. Photo by Clinton Brandhagen

Ghosts of These Historical Moments

Collier’s script shifted seamlessly between periods, drawing parallels between the veterans’ 1932 protests and the significant demonstrations of the late 20th century. These scenes explored the continuous fight for economic equality, racial justice, and opposition to war, illustrating how the echoes of past struggles resonate through the decades. The thematic examination of political upheaval and economic uncertainty underscored the cyclical nature of societal challenges, emphasizing that the ghosts of these historical moments continue to inhabit and influence our present-day realities.

Lynn Hawley and Jose-Maria Aguila in a scene from A Hundred Circling Camps by Sam Collier at the Atlantic Theater Company Stage 2 in New York City. Photo by Clinton Brandhagen

Enduring Relevance

Rebecca Wear’s direction ensured the transitions between eras were fluid and lucid. At the same time, the performances by both student and veteran actors were uniform, bringing profundity and validity to the multi-layered characters. The production’s capacity to highlight the timelessness of the struggle for justice and equality was particularly poignant, leaving the audience to reflect on the enduring relevance of these issues and the means for resolution.

Maggie Blake, Lynn Hawley, and Zack Maluccio in a scene from A Hundred Circling Camps by Sam Collier at the Atlantic Theater Company Stage 2 in New York City. Photo by Clinton Brandhagen

Power of Theater

A Hundred Circling Camps is a historical recount and a mirror reflecting the ongoing battles for social justice and equality. The Dogteam Theatre Project’s presentation of this play is a testament to the power of theater to connect past and present, reminding us of the sacrifices and work still to be done. This production is a significant contribution to contemporary theatre that leaves a lasting impact on its audience.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

First, I want to talk about Dogteam Theatre Project and commend them and their inaugural season as the producers of La Viuda by María Irene Fornés. They are an offshoot of the theater program at Middlebury College in Vermont and are putting on two plays in rep at Atlantic Stage 2 (that in itself is a big bone to chew) La Viuda (which I saw) and A Hundred Circling Camps. Their purpose is to give the opportunity for college students to work directly with professionals in creating work for the theater. There’s no question there’s a lot of heart here, in the project as well as what they put up on stage.

As it’s their first, they chose to produce the first play by María Irene Fornés written in 1961, La Viuda (The Widow). If you don’t know much about “Irene,” please click on the link. She was a formidable playwright in her time influencing Shepard, Kushner, Vogel, Wilson, Albee in theirs, and received nine Obie Theatre Awards and was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize in Drama in 1990. Her work, though not her acclaim, was major in the New York theater scene for decades.

The setup of La Viuda: Angela (Jay Romero) spends 30 years in self-exile in Seville, Spain, encompassing the years of the Spanish American War and the Cuban War of Independence from Spain. She is in constant correspondence with her lawyer back in Cuba trying to maintain the status quo of her previous life, her family, marital status, and staying constant with her other relationships. With a time delay of ten minutes, imagine trying to tell someone how to drive a car for the first time, with your children in it, via text. That type of frustration is constant in the letter exchange that went on for years. The ghosts of her past (herself-included) haunt her in the drawing room where she both dictates and reads the letters throughout the course of the play and eventually taunt her for the role of victim that she has taken on, lamenting and embracing the role of widow. Though she contests that she is fighting for her dignity, it’s victimhood for the role life has cast her in that she embraces.

La Viuda is a play that is not done very much as it is difficult to do, mostly a monologue of the two sides of a letter correspondence. The frustration with the distance and the feeling of powerlessness to do anything about it is in much of the writing and makes it hard to sit through as it plays one note. What does come across most objectively, is Angela’s sense of injustice and the struggle to keep going and persevering despite. There is a nice use of a crotalus to comment on the times that she is lying to herself.

Historically, this is a play worth seeing in the context that it is the first of the 40 plays that María Irene Fornés wrote.

———–

La Viuda, by María Irene Fornés, was translated and directed by Olga Sanchez Saltveit.

The cast includes Jose-Maria Aguila, Zack Maluccio, Jesse Muñoz, Jay Romero, Fidel Vicioso, Bri Beach, Ethan Fleming, Jacob Joseph Medina, Zeph Santiago, and Katelyn Wenkoff.

Marck Evancho, scenic design, Summer Lee Jack, costume design, Calvin Anderson, Lighting design, and Madison Middleton, sound design.

Tickets can be bought here.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

The first 5 or so minutes of “Inspired By True Events” by Ryan Spahn, we watch as Mary (Dana Scurlock), the stage manager for this woe-begotten theatre company in Rochester, completes the thankless job of cleaning up after the actors.   She covers all the minuscule bases.  Emptying out the coffee filter of cold grounds.  Dumping the old coffee in a nearby slop sink.  Rinsing the coffee pot.  Filling it with water.  Emptying the new water into the well of the coffee maker.  Filling the fresh filter with new coffee grounds.  Placing said filter into the coffee maker.  Turning the coffee maker on. In addition, she tosses the food containers, takes out the trash and places a new bag in the trash can.

In some ways this is the most fascinating part of the play.  The task at hand is clear, and the actor performs her duty very well.  Trash and old coffee are the obstacles, and she dispenses with everything before she lets herself enjoy a cup of Joe,

Let me say right off the bat that these actors are doing the best they can.  The text they have to work with, however, combined with an absence of directorial guidance, sends them off the rails where they remain moored in a swamp of, well I don’t know what.

The one bit of life in the play is Mallory Portnoy as Eileen, who is self referential in the extreme.  The play they are performing has just opened to the best reviews ever (we never find out what the play is about even though we see bits of it on the in-house monitor), and tonight’s performance is sold out.  This could mean an extended run which would show those other theatre people who is who in Rochester.  Fresh from a biking accident (it was the car driver’s fault for not seeing her of course) Eileen arrives at the theatre hyped up on adrenaline and ready to take on anyone who gets in her way. She doles out empathy and sympathy when it is convenient and/or important for her.  And she is sparing with the doses.  Here, Spahn’s writing gives Eileen enough layers and nuances that Portnoy can create a whole person with some nice comedic touches.  Eileen is the embodiment of the actor we all want to avoid – especially if we are sharing a dressing room with them.

Funny thing about that – the program notes tell us that all 35 people crammed together in the tiny audience space are sitting in the actual Green Room (actors’ reception area) of the Out Of The Box Theatre.  Even the characters call it a Green Room.  What is odd about that is that the tiny cast puts on makeup and changes into costumes in this little space that – and that makes it a dressing room.  Hmmmnnn.

There are other inconsistencies – why does Mary mention she is going to a wedding but never leaves?  What was the crash in the “Other” dressing room?   Were there mice in the vent?  Will Robert (Lou Libertore) ever stop steaming his shirt?  And why can we barely understand Colin (Jack DiFalco) in the final very important scene of this play?

The lack of depth in Spahn’s writing overall leaves gaping holes in this story.  But even those could be addressed were Knud Adams direction forthcoming in how to create characters with needs and challenges.  As it was, all the tiny audience of 35 could do was watch the actors pass the time while we counted the minutes until this production wound down and coasted into the station where we would be allowed to disembark.  As we exited the theatre, even the blistering heat felt refreshing.

Inspired By True Events by actor/writer Ryan Spahn, directed by Knud Adams

WITH Jack Difalco as Colin, Lou Liberatore as Robert, Mallory Portnoy as Eileen and Dana Scurlock  as Mary.

Scenic design by Lindsay Fuori, costume design by Siena Zoë Allen, lighting design by Paige Seber, sound design by Peter Mills Weiss and props design by Sean Frank. Technical Director is Sajari Hume. Production Management is by Out of the Box Theatrics.

Through August 4.  Tickets HERE

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: The Delicate Tears of the Waning Moon (Las Dedicadas Lágrimas de la Luna Menguante)

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

The Delicate Tears of the Waning Moon (Las Dedicadas Lágrimas de la Luna Menguante) currently playing at Teatro Repertorio Españo, is heartfelt and heart-rending.  Inspired by true events historical human rights violations in Venezuela, it is the story of the harrowing consequences of speaking out against injustice.

As the play opens Rodrigo (a sweetly vulnerable Fernando Then) wheels Paulina (a fiercely beautiful Rebeca Alemán, in a tour-de-force performance) onstage.  Both journalists, Rodrigo and Paulina are colleagues and friends.  Paulina has built her career writing of the epic brutality and femicide occurring in her country, particularly that suffered by its indigenous peoples.  Paulina’s outspoken reporting has made her the target of the forces of violence and impunity, resulting in an attack which has left her partially paralyzed, confined to a wheelchair, and barely able to speak.

Gentle, lyrical music flows like an undercurrent as Rodrigo and Paulina slowly circle the stage as if on an imaginary path, one which, as the lights go up, has led her home.  In her living room turned bedroom, Paulina sleeps among the memories of which she has been robbed.  Endlessly patient, Rodrigo devotes himself to her recovery, both physical and mental.  He gently assists her getting into her bed.  He gives her water, makes her comfortable, doing all the mundane tasks she cannot attend to herself.  They work together with flashcards to combat Paulina’s aphasia.  As she struggles to read aloud, one feels her frustration.

As the story unfolds and Paulina begins to recover her memory, you almost wish she had not.  The details of brutality, sexual assault and mutilation revealed sicken one.  And yet it’s real.  Women  have faced this kind of treatment, in some form or another,  throughout history – the “Disappears” in Argentina and Chile, genocidal rape during the war in Bosnia, the women of Juarez, Mexico, living in constant fear of ending up behind a dumpster, Israeli women kidnapped by Hamas in the October 7th assault.  As ever, women’s bodies are the battlefield across which men’s wars are waged – whether officially declared, or the implicit war of relentless ad hoc violence.

Iraida Tapias has directed this devastating story in a manner that is both unflinching and lacking in melodrama, although it is at times a bit loud.  Tapias leans into the horror even as she underplays the various milestones in Paulina’s recovery.  In the naturalistic way in which she has the characters move about the stage, Tapias subtly develops Paulina’s recovered memory without fanfare, leaving space for her return to life, as it were, to be all the more devastating.  It’s as if Paulina has been out of focus, and suddenly we see her.  We witness the dedicated journalist returning to her body.
Omayra Garriga Casiano’s lighting keeps it real, giving Marisabel Muñoz Rodriguez’ homey set a familiar feel in warm reds and yellows, as differentiated from the spotlight of cool blue for Paulina’s interior world.  Stephanie Rodrigues’ projections hint at the outside world, with glowing sunspaces or the unencumbered flickering of butterfly wings.  Atmospheric music by Lester Paredes and Ludwig Paredes wraps the mood in melody.
Many Venezualan journalists have risked their lives speaking up against the continued cruelty experienced by women throughout their country, and the fact that it continually goes unpunished.  It is the kind of speech audacious in a criminal environment.  Venezuelans, particularly women and indigenous peoples, have become trapped in the clutches of the corruption and impunity brought about by the immunity of those in power.  In a just world, no-one would be above the law, but we live in unjust times.

The Delicate Tears of the Waning Moon (Las Dedicadas Lágrimas de la Luna Menguante), written by Rebeca Alemán and directed by Iraida Tapias; featuring Rebeca Alemán and Fernando Then.  Set and costume design by Marisabel Muñoz Rodriguez.  Original music by Lester Paredes and Ludwig Paredes.  Lighting design by Omayra Garriga Casiano; projection design by Stephanie Rodrigues.

Presented in Spanish with English supertitlesPlease note:  If the English supertitles appear above the stage audience right.  If you need them, it is best to sit in that area.

Produced by Water People Theater (WPT).

At Teatro Repertorio Español, 138 E. 27th Street, NYC through Sunday, July 21, 2024. Tickets start at $27 and are available at www.repertorio.nyc.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.
